meta.blurb: The crowd at the sale is angry about heavy taxes, and everyone wants old Father Abraham to speak. His answer is a string of sharp little sayings about time, debt and idle hands. Benjamin Franklin wrote it, and it still stings.
meta.bible:
Benjamin Franklin: American printer, writer and scientist, born in Boston in 1706, who worked in Philadelphia. Poor Richard's Almanack: the yearly book that Franklin published for about twenty-five years, ending with the edition for 1758. Poor Richard and Richard Saunders: the invented author of the almanack. Father Abraham: the plain, white-haired old man in the tale who speaks to the crowd. The Way to Wealth: the speech, first printed in the 1758 almanack and later published on its own. Vendue: a public sale of goods, where people bid. Heaven: the power the old man says we must also depend on. Job: a man in the Bible who suffered and was later prosperous. Lent: the forty days of fasting before Easter. Easter: the Christian spring festival. Spain: the country named in the speech. Indies: the lands from which Spain received gold. Reason: the old man's word for good sense. Many of the sayings are older proverbs that Franklin reworded. Voice and tone: lively, witty, practical and kind; the old sayings are paraphrased in plain modern English; no invented numbers or quotes. Josiah Franklin: Benjamin's father, who made soap and candles in Boston. James Franklin: Benjamin's older brother, a Boston printer to whom he was apprenticed at twelve. Silence Dogood: the made-up name under which the boy Franklin wrote letters for his brother's newspaper. Junto: the club of friends Franklin formed in Philadelphia in 1727 to discuss ideas and improve themselves. Pennsylvania Gazette: the newspaper Franklin took over in 1729. Library Company: the lending library Franklin and friends began in 1731. Bridget: the wife of the invented Richard Saunders. Titan Leeds: a rival almanack maker whose death Franklin playfully predicted for 1733. Deborah Read: Franklin's wife. Almanack: a yearly book of calendar, weather and sayings. Bonhomme Richard: French for Good Man Richard, the French name for Poor Richard, and the name of John Paul Jones's warship in 1779. John Paul Jones: American naval officer. France: where Franklin lived as an American envoy. London: the English capital. Autobiography: the life story Franklin wrote. Britain: the king's country. England: the country of the king.
 Union Fire Company: the volunteer fire company Franklin helped start in Philadelphia in 1736. Pennsylvania Hospital: the hospital founded in Philadelphia in 1751 with Dr Thomas Bond. Thomas Bond: Philadelphia doctor and friend of Franklin. Philosopher: the philosopher's stone was a legendary substance that alchemists believed would turn lead into gold. Alchemists: early students of chemistry who sought it. Declaration of Independence: the 1776 document announcing American freedom from British rule. Treaty of Paris: the 1783 peace that ended the war with Britain. La Science du Bonhomme Richard: the French title of the sayings in the 1770s. Philadelphia: the city where Franklin lived. Pennsylvania: the colony Franklin served. Atlantic: the ocean. Europe: the continent. Paris: the French capital. Franklin died on 17 April 1790, aged eighty-four.

beats.scene: Benjamin Franklin inks a printing press in his busy Philadelphia shop
beats.summary: Benjamin Franklin, a printer in Philadelphia, published a yearly book called Poor Richard's Almanack.

beats.scene: A small boy sits among many children in a Boston house hung with candles
beats.summary: Franklin was born in Boston in 1706, the youngest son in a very large family whose father made soap and candles.

beats.scene: A boy reads a thick book by candlelight while the house sleeps
beats.summary: Benjamin went to school for only about two years, but he loved books and read at every chance.

beats.scene: A twelve-year-old boy sets metal letters in a frame beside a heavy press
beats.summary: At twelve he became an apprentice to his older brother James, a printer, and learned to set type.

beats.scene: A boy quietly slides a letter under the door of a dark print shop
beats.summary: Using the made-up name Silence Dogood, the teenage Franklin wrote funny letters that his brother printed without knowing who the author was.

beats.scene: A young man steps aboard a small boat leaving Boston harbour
beats.summary: After quarrels with James, Benjamin left Boston by boat in 1723, at seventeen, to start a new life in Philadelphia.

beats.scene: A tired young man walks a Philadelphia street with a roll under each arm
beats.summary: Franklin arrived in Philadelphia tired and almost penniless, and he wrote that he bought bread rolls and walked up the street eating one.

beats.scene: A young printer sets type by lamplight in a small Philadelphia workshop
beats.summary: He found work with a Philadelphia printer, worked hard, and within a few years he had a printing house of his own.

beats.scene: A group of friends talks around a table in a Philadelphia room
beats.summary: In 1727 he formed the Junto, a club of friends who met to discuss ideas and help each other improve.

beats.scene: Readers borrow books from shelves in a small lending library
beats.summary: He took over a newspaper, the Pennsylvania Gazette, and with friends began the Library Company, a lending library.

beats.scene: Franklin hands a customer the first copy of a brand-new almanack
beats.summary: In December 1732 Franklin printed the first Poor Richard's Almanack, for the year 1733, under the name Richard Saunders.

beats.scene: A poor stargazer at a cluttered desk while his wife stands at the door
beats.summary: Franklin borrowed the name of an English almanack maker and gave his Richard a wife, Bridget, who wished he would earn more money.

beats.scene: A farmer's wife reads a calendar printed with moon phases and weather
beats.summary: An almanack held a calendar, guesses about the weather and useful facts for farmers and families.

beats.scene: A printer fills the small gaps between calendar days with short sayings
beats.summary: Poor Richard filled the spare spaces on the calendar pages with short, witty sayings about work, saving and money.

beats.scene: A writer compares old proverbs in several languages on his desk
beats.summary: Many of the sayings were old proverbs from different countries that Franklin reworded, and others were his own.

beats.scene: A man in a nightcap reads an almanack that announces his own death
beats.summary: Franklin teased a rival almanack maker, Titan Leeds, by predicting in print that Leeds would die on a day in October 1733.

beats.scene: A grumpy man waves a pamphlet while Richard calls him a ghost
beats.summary: Leeds protested that he was still alive, and Poor Richard answered that the angry writer must be a fraud or a ghost.

beats.scene: Villagers gather around a fireside while a boy reads aloud from the almanack
beats.summary: The almanack sold in thousands, as many as ten thousand copies in a year by one old estimate, and its sayings were repeated everywhere.

beats.scene: Franklin gathers sheets of sayings into one neat bundle at his desk
beats.summary: After about twenty-five years, for the almanack of 1758, Franklin gathered the best sayings into a single speech wrapped in a little story.

beats.scene: The printed speech travels in a bundle on a cart along a country road
beats.summary: Later printers published the speech on its own and called it The Way to Wealth, and it spread through many countries.

beats.scene: Richard Saunders sits at his desk writing a preface by candlelight
beats.summary: In his preface Richard says that nothing pleases an author more than to be quoted by other learned writers.

beats.scene: A weary almanack maker looks at a plate of pudding and shrugs
beats.summary: Richard says other almanack makers rarely praised him, and that without the solid pudding his book earned him he would have been discouraged.

beats.scene: Richard rides along a village road and overhears two men talking
beats.summary: Richard decides that ordinary people are the best judges, since they buy his book, and on his travels he often heard his sayings repeated.

beats.scene: Richard reads one of his own sayings aloud with a very solemn face
beats.summary: Richard admits that, to encourage the habit of repeating good sayings, he has sometimes quoted himself with great seriousness.

beats.scene: Richard reins in his horse near a large crowd at a country sale
beats.summary: Richard says that he was gratified by something that happened lately, when he stopped his horse at a vendue of merchants' goods.

beats.scene: Goods piled on tables while a crowd waits for the sale
beats.summary: The hour of sale had not yet come, and the people were talking about the badness of the times.

beats.scene: Worried neighbours study a tax paper beside a farm cart
beats.summary: Taxes and prices were high, since in the 1750s the colonies were at war with France and its allies, and war costs a great deal of money.

beats.scene: A plain, clean old man with white hair listens at the crowd's edge
beats.summary: Among the crowd stood a plain, clean old man with white hair, known to the people as Father Abraham.

beats.scene: A worried man in the crowd turns and calls to the old man
beats.summary: One of the crowd asked Father Abraham what he thought of the times, whether the taxes would ruin the country, how they could pay and what to do.

beats.scene: Father Abraham rises slowly and the crowd gathers close around him
beats.summary: Father Abraham stood up and promised short advice, since a word to the wise is enough and many words will not fill a bushel.

beats.scene: Father Abraham speaks gravely to neighbours gathered in the open air
beats.summary: Father Abraham began by agreeing that the taxes were very heavy, and said they would be easier to pay if the government's taxes were the only ones.

beats.scene: Three heaped bags of coins labelled idleness, pride and folly sit on a table
beats.summary: But we have many other taxes, he said, and worse ones: we are taxed twice as much by idleness, three times as much by pride and four times as much by folly.

beats.scene: A tax officer shrugs and closes his ledger in front of a crowd
beats.summary: No government commissioner can ease or lift those taxes, he said, so no one can ask for a reduction.

beats.scene: A man listens closely, one hand cupped behind his ear
beats.summary: Even so, Father Abraham said, good advice can help, and God helps those who help themselves, as Poor Richard says.

beats.scene: One neighbour grumbles beside the fire while another mends his fence
beats.summary: He pictured two neighbours in a hard year, one who grumbled by the fire and one who got up and mended his fence.

beats.scene: A clerk counts hours into piles beside an idle man
beats.summary: He said that people would think it a hard government that took a tenth of their time, but idleness takes much more than that.

beats.scene: A tired man lies in bed in the middle of a bright working day
beats.summary: He added that sloth, by bringing on diseases, shortens life.

beats.scene: A rusty old plough stands abandoned in tall grass beside a barn
beats.summary: Sloth, like rust, wears us out faster than work does.

beats.scene: A bright brass key turns smoothly in a well-used lock
beats.summary: The key that is used every day is always bright.

beats.scene: Men in the crowd look at their own rough hands and shift uneasily
beats.summary: Some of the listeners shifted uneasily, since they knew that they had spent idle days, and the old man turned to the matter of time.

beats.scene: An hourglass on a desk with the last sand running through
beats.summary: If you love life, said Father Abraham, do not squander time, for time is the stuff that life is made of.

beats.scene: A man snores in bed while sunlight pours through the window
beats.summary: How much more time than is necessary we spend in sleep, he said, forgetting that sleep costs hours we could use.

beats.scene: A fox sleeps in the sun outside an unguarded henhouse
beats.summary: He quoted the saying that the sleeping fox catches no poultry.

beats.scene: A churchyard under a calm sky, with long grass between the stones
beats.summary: There will be sleeping enough in the grave, he added, so we should not sleep away the hours we could use for work.

beats.scene: A banker weighs a bag of gold against a small glass of sand
beats.summary: If time is the most precious thing, he said, then wasting it must be the greatest waste of all.

beats.scene: A woman searches an empty cupboard for something she has misplaced
beats.summary: Lost time, said Father Abraham, is never found again.

beats.scene: A man puts off a job while the day slips away on a clock
beats.summary: What we call time enough, he said, always proves little enough.

beats.scene: Farmers roll up their sleeves and set out together at dawn
beats.summary: Let us then be up and doing, he said, and doing to the purpose, so that by diligence we do more with less trouble.

beats.scene: Two men face the same task, one struggling and one working smoothly
beats.summary: Sloth makes all things difficult, he said, but industry makes all things easy.

beats.scene: A man trots down a muddy road after his business, far behind the day
beats.summary: He who rises late must trot all day and will scarcely catch his business at night, for laziness travels so slowly that poverty soon overtakes it.

beats.scene: A farmer leads a team of oxen and walks ahead of them
beats.summary: Drive your business, said Father Abraham, and do not let it drive you; early to bed and early to rise makes a man healthy, wealthy and wise.

beats.scene: A man gazes at the horizon while his field lies unploughed behind him
beats.summary: What is the use of hoping for better times, he asked, when we can make the times better if we bestir ourselves?

beats.scene: An empty table with a bowl and spoon, and a man waiting
beats.summary: Industry need not wish, he said, and he that lives upon hope will die fasting.

beats.scene: Two strong hands grip a heavy hoe in a field of stones
beats.summary: There are no gains without pains, he said, so help hands, for I have no lands, or if I have, they are smartly taxed.

beats.scene: A shoemaker bends over a boot with a hammer in a tidy workshop
beats.summary: He that has a trade has an estate, he said, because a skill is worth as much as land.

beats.scene: A tailor stitches carefully in a shop under a painted sign
beats.summary: He that has a calling has an office of profit and honour, but the trade must be worked at and the calling followed well.

beats.scene: Hunger peers in through a window at a busy, well-fed household
beats.summary: If we are industrious we shall never starve, for hunger looks in at the working man's house but dares not enter.

beats.scene: A constable stops at a tidy door and turns away
beats.summary: Nor will the bailiff or the constable enter, for industry pays debts, while despair increases them.

beats.scene: A hopeful farmer stands at his gate looking at a large field
beats.summary: Even if you have found no treasure and no rich relation left you a legacy, diligence is the mother of good luck, and God gives all things to industry.

beats.scene: A farmer ploughs deep furrows at dawn while a man sleeps under a tree
beats.summary: Plough deep while sluggards sleep, he said, and you will have corn to sell and to keep.

beats.scene: A man closes his ledger at day's end beside a clear window
beats.summary: Work while it is called today, said Father Abraham, for you do not know how much you may be hindered tomorrow.

beats.scene: Two heaps of tools stand side by side on a workbench, one larger
beats.summary: One today is worth two tomorrows, he said.

beats.scene: A man crosses a task off a long list pinned on a barn door
beats.summary: If you have something to do tomorrow, do it today.

beats.scene: A servant lowers his eyes as a stern master finds him sitting idle
beats.summary: If you were a servant, he asked, would you not be ashamed if a good master caught you idle?

beats.scene: A man scolds himself in front of a mirror in a busy house
beats.summary: You are your own master, he said, so be ashamed to catch yourself idle when there is so much to do for yourself, your family and your country.

beats.scene: A cat in a pair of tiny gloves sits helpless beside a mouse hole
beats.summary: Handle your tools without mittens, he said, for the cat in gloves catches no mice.

beats.scene: Water drips steadily onto a hollow in a stone
beats.summary: There is much to be done, he said, and you may feel weak, but stick to it steadily and you will see great results, for constant dropping wears away stones.

beats.scene: A small mouse gnaws through a thick rope on a ship's deck
beats.summary: By diligence and patience, he said, the mouse ate in two the cable.

beats.scene: A woodcutter swings his axe at a great oak, with chips flying
beats.summary: Little strokes fell great oaks, he said.

beats.scene: A man rests in a garden chair after finishing his work
beats.summary: Asked whether a man must have no leisure, Father Abraham said to use time well in order to gain leisure, and not to throw away an hour, since you are not sure of a minute.

beats.scene: A woman sits at ease on a porch with her finished work beside her
beats.summary: Leisure is time for doing something useful, he said, and the diligent man will gain it, but the lazy man never will.

beats.scene: A man in a hammock beside a man reading a book in a garden
beats.summary: A life of leisure and a life of laziness, he said, are two different things.

beats.scene: A man in fine clothes sits at a card table with an empty purse
beats.summary: Many people, he said, would live by their wits alone without labour, but they break for want of stock.

beats.scene: A man works contentedly as a bright butterfly follows him through a field
beats.summary: Fly pleasures, he said, and they will follow you.

beats.scene: A woman spins wool beside a chest full of folded linen
beats.summary: The diligent spinner has a large shift, he said, meaning that the busy woman is well supplied with clothes.

beats.scene: Neighbours tip their hats to a prosperous farmer with a cow and sheep
beats.summary: Now that I have a sheep and a cow, everybody bids me good morrow, he said, for people greet those who have some property.

beats.scene: A shopkeeper counts his stock himself while workers stack crates behind him
beats.summary: But with industry we must also be steady, settled and careful, and oversee our own affairs with our own eyes, not trusting too much to others.

beats.scene: An old oak stands firm beside a house that has stood for years
beats.summary: He never saw an oft-removed tree, nor an oft-removed family, that throve so well as those that settled be.

beats.scene: A family hurriedly carries their belongings out of a burning house
beats.summary: Three removes, he said, are as bad as a fire.

beats.scene: A shopkeeper sweeps his own front step before opening for the day
beats.summary: Keep your shop, he said, and your shop will keep you.

beats.scene: A merchant walks to a distant warehouse himself while a messenger waits
beats.summary: If you would have your business done, go; if not, send.

beats.scene: A ploughman walks behind the plough, guiding it with both hands
beats.summary: He that by the plough would thrive, he said, must either hold or drive himself.

beats.scene: A master looks sharply over a worker's shoulder in a busy shop
beats.summary: The eye of the master, he said, will do more work than both his hands.

beats.scene: A learned man with books and a careless man sit at two desks
beats.summary: Want of care, he said, does us more damage than want of knowledge.

beats.scene: A farmer's purse lies open on a table while workmen drift away
beats.summary: Not to oversee workmen, he said, is to leave them your purse open.

beats.scene: A trusting man hands his keys to a stranger with a smile
beats.summary: Trusting too much to other people's care ruins many, he said, for in worldly affairs a careful doubt protects a man better than blind trust.

beats.scene: A man happily sweeps his own workshop floor at dawn
beats.summary: A man's own care is profitable, he said, for if you want a faithful servant that you like, you should serve yourself.

beats.scene: A rider examines his horse's hooves in a stable yard
beats.summary: A little neglect may breed great mischief, he said, and he quoted a rhyme about a lost nail.

beats.scene: A horseshoe nail lies in the dust beside a fallen rider
beats.summary: For want of a nail the shoe was lost, then the horse, then the rider, and all for the lack of care over one small piece of iron.

beats.scene: Father Abraham pauses and then raises a finger to the crowd
beats.summary: So much for industry and attention to one's own business, he said, but frugality must be added if industry is to be more certainly successful.

beats.scene: A worker bends over a spinning grindstone, his nose close to the wheel
beats.summary: A man who does not know how to save as he earns may keep his nose to the grindstone all his life and die not worth a groat.

beats.scene: A heavy table groans with food beside a thin, folded will on a shelf
beats.summary: A fat kitchen makes a lean will, he said.

beats.scene: A farmer sells a field while his barns stand empty
beats.summary: Many estates are spent in the getting, he said, since too many people spend what they earn faster than they earn it.

beats.scene: A spinning wheel stands unused while a family drinks tea at a table
beats.summary: He said that women had left their spinning and knitting for tea, and men their hewing and splitting for punch.

beats.scene: A man holds a purse in one hand and a pen in the other
beats.summary: If you would be wealthy, he said, think of saving as well as of getting.

beats.scene: A ship loaded with gold sails away from an empty harbour in Spain
beats.summary: The Indies have not made Spain rich, he said, because her spending was greater than her income.

beats.scene: A man sweeps fancy hats and ornaments out of his front door
beats.summary: Away with expensive follies, he said, and you will have less cause to complain of hard times, heavy taxes and costly families.

beats.scene: Dice, a wine bottle and cards lie on a table beside an empty purse
beats.summary: Wine, gambling and deceit, he said, make the wealth small and the want great.

beats.scene: A man looks from a bottle to two hungry children
beats.summary: What maintains one vice, he said, would bring up two children.

beats.scene: A small tea table with a little cake and a glass of punch
beats.summary: You may think a little tea, a little punch, a finer meal or finer clothes now and then is no great matter, he said.

beats.scene: Coins drop one by one into a jar until it is nearly full
beats.summary: Many a little makes a mickle, he said, meaning that small amounts add up to a large one.

beats.scene: Water seeps through a small crack in the side of a great ship
beats.summary: Beware of little expenses, he said, for a small leak will sink a great ship.

beats.scene: A man in a good coat eats a sweet pastry while a beggar watches
beats.summary: Who dainties love shall beggars prove, he said.

beats.scene: A rich man throws a lavish feast while a quiet neighbour eats leftovers
beats.summary: Fools make feasts, he said, and wise men eat them.

beats.scene: Bargain hunters examine piles of cloth, ornaments and gadgets at the sale
beats.summary: Here at this sale, he said, you are all gathered to buy fineries and knick-knacks, which you call goods, but which may prove to be evils.

beats.scene: A buyer holds a low price tag beside a mound of unneeded goods
beats.summary: You expect that the goods will be sold cheap, he said, but if you have no need of them, they are dear to you.

beats.scene: A man sells his bed to a dealer in a bare room
beats.summary: Buy what you have no need of, he said, and before long you will sell what you do need.

beats.scene: A shopper stops at a stall and frowns at a very low price
beats.summary: At a great pennyworth pause a while, he said, since the cheapness may only seem real, or the bargain may strain your business.

beats.scene: A man sits sadly among cheap goods that he cannot use or sell
beats.summary: Many have been ruined, Poor Richard says, by buying good pennyworths.

beats.scene: A buyer clutches a parcel with a sorry face at a crowded sale
beats.summary: It is foolish to lay out money in a purchase of repentance, and yet this folly is practised every day at sales for want of minding the almanack.

beats.scene: A woman in a fine new dress cooks a thin soup for hungry children
beats.summary: Many a person, he said, has gone with a hungry belly for the sake of finery on the back, and half-starved a family.

beats.scene: A bright silk dress hangs over a cold, empty kitchen fireplace
beats.summary: Silks and satins, scarlet and velvet, put out the kitchen fire, as Poor Richard says.

beats.scene: A shopkeeper shows rolls of coloured cloth to a longing customer
beats.summary: These things are not the necessaries of life, he said, and can scarcely be called conveniences, yet because they look pretty, how many people want them.

beats.scene: A short list of needs hangs beside a very long list of wants
beats.summary: In this way, he said, the artificial wants of mankind become more numerous than the natural ones.

beats.scene: One poor family stands among a crowd of a hundred needy people
beats.summary: For one poor person, he said, there are a hundred indigent, meaning that the wants we invent make many people feel poor.

beats.scene: A gentleman in a worn velvet coat humbly asks his neighbour for a loan
beats.summary: By such extravagance, he said, the genteel are brought to poverty and forced to borrow from those they once despised, who kept their footing by industry and frugality.

beats.scene: A farmer in muddy boots stands tall beside a gentleman kneeling in the dust
beats.summary: A ploughman on his legs, he said, is higher than a gentleman on his knees.

beats.scene: A young heir looks over a large inherited house with a careless smile
beats.summary: Perhaps they have had a small estate left to them, which they never worked to get, so they think it will always be day and never night.

beats.scene: A man scoops the last flour from the bottom of an empty meal tub
beats.summary: Always taking out of the meal tub, and never putting in, he said, soon comes to the bottom.

beats.scene: A family stands around a dry well with empty buckets
beats.summary: Then, as Poor Richard says, when the well is dry they know the worth of water.

beats.scene: A man knocks on a neighbour's door with his hat in his hand
beats.summary: If you would know the value of money, he said, go and try to borrow some.

beats.scene: A sad borrower and a worried lender look at one empty purse
beats.summary: He that goes a-borrowing goes a-sorrowing, he said, and so does the lender when he goes to get his money back.

beats.scene: A tailor shows fine cloth to a man who checks his purse
beats.summary: Poor Richard says that fond pride of dress is a very curse, and that before you consult your fancy you should consult your purse.

beats.scene: A fashionably dressed man stands loudly demanding charity on a street corner
beats.summary: Pride, he said, is as loud a beggar as want, and a great deal more saucy.

beats.scene: A man in a new hat looks down at his old shoes and sighs
beats.summary: When you have bought one fine thing, he said, you must buy ten more, so that your appearance may be all of a piece.

beats.scene: A man holds up one hand to refuse a long line of shop goods
beats.summary: It is easier to suppress the first desire than to satisfy all those that follow it, said Poor Dick.

beats.scene: A small frog swells its body beside a huge ox in a field
beats.summary: It is as truly folly for the poor to ape the rich as for the frog to swell in order to equal the ox.

beats.scene: A great ship rides far out while small boats stay near the shore
beats.summary: Large vessels may venture more, he said, but little boats should keep near the shore.

beats.scene: A peacock struts with a proud head while a crowd mutters at the back
beats.summary: Yet the folly is soon punished, he said, for pride that dines on vanity sups on contempt.

beats.scene: Three meals at a table: a feast, a plain dinner and an empty plate
beats.summary: And in another place, he said, pride breakfasted with Plenty, dined with Poverty and supped with Infamy.

beats.scene: A well-dressed man stands before a mirror, then looks at his bills
beats.summary: After all, he asked, what use is this pride of appearance, for which so much is risked and so much is suffered?

beats.scene: A sick man in fine clothes lies in bed, wincing in pain
beats.summary: Pride of appearance, he said, cannot promote health nor ease pain.

beats.scene: A rival gazes sourly at a showy neighbour from a window
beats.summary: It makes no increase of merit in the person, he said, but it creates envy and hastens misfortune.

beats.scene: A man signs a paper at a shop counter while a clerk smiles
beats.summary: But what madness it must be, he said, to run in debt for these superfluities.

beats.scene: A sign at the vendue offers six months' credit to all buyers
beats.summary: The terms of this sale offer six months' credit, he said, which tempts people who cannot spare ready money to hope to be fine without it.

beats.scene: A heavy chain runs from a man's wrist to a lender's hand
beats.summary: But think what you do when you run in debt, he said: you give another person power over your liberty.

beats.scene: A debtor in the street turns pale and hides when he sees his creditor
beats.summary: If you cannot pay at the time, he said, you will be ashamed to see your creditor and fearful when you speak to him.

beats.scene: A debtor at his door makes humble excuses to a patient creditor
beats.summary: You will make poor, pitiful, sneaking excuses, he said, and by degrees lose your honesty and sink into plain lying.

beats.scene: A man looks down a long staircase, with debt at the top
beats.summary: For, as Poor Richard says, the second vice is lying, and the first is running in debt.

beats.scene: A free man walks tall through a town and greets everyone he meets
beats.summary: Lying rides upon debt's back, he said, whereas a free person ought not to be ashamed or afraid to see or speak to anyone.

beats.scene: A thin man holds an empty cloth bag that sags on the ground
beats.summary: Poverty, he said, often robs a man of spirit and virtue, for it is hard for an empty bag to stand upright.

beats.scene: A royal messenger reads out a decree on a town's market square
beats.summary: He asked what they would think of a prince who forbade them, on pain of prison or servitude, to dress like a gentleman or gentlewoman.

B1B2: Benjamin Franklin was a busy printer in Philadelphia, a city in the American colonies. Every year he also made a small book called Poor Richard's Almanack, which many families bought.
Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston in 1706, the youngest son in a very large family. His father, Josiah, made soap and candles, and money was always tight at home.
Benjamin went to school for only about two years, because his father needed his help and could not pay for more. He loved books so much that he read whatever he could borrow, often late at night.
When he was twelve, Benjamin became an apprentice to his older brother James, who was a printer in Boston. He learned to set tiny metal letters into rows and to work the heavy press.

When he was about sixteen, Benjamin wrote funny letters for his brother's newspaper, using the made-up name Silence Dogood. He slid them under the shop door at night, and James printed them without knowing who the writer was.

Benjamin and James often quarrelled, because James had a hot temper, and the young man grew tired of working for him. In 1723, at the age of seventeen, he left Boston by boat and headed for Philadelphia.
Franklin reached Philadelphia tired, dirty and almost without money in his pocket. He wrote later that he bought three large rolls and walked up the street with one under each arm, eating the third.

Franklin found work with a printer in Philadelphia and worked harder than almost anyone in the shop. Within a few years he had saved enough, with help from friends, to open a printing house of his own.
In 1727 Franklin started a club called the Junto, where friends met every week to talk about ideas and how to improve their town. The members also helped each other with their different businesses.

In 1729 Franklin took over a newspaper called the Pennsylvania Gazette, and he made it lively. A few years later he and his friends began the Library Company, where members shared books that no one could afford alone.
In December 1732 Franklin printed the first Poor Richard's Almanack, which was meant for the year 1733. He did not put his own name on it, but the name Richard Saunders.

Franklin borrowed the name Richard Saunders from an English almanack maker of the century before. His Richard was a poor man who studied the stars, and his wife, Bridget, wished that he would earn more money.
An almanack was a yearly book with a calendar, the phases of the moon and guesses about the weather. Farmers used it to decide when to plant, and families kept it near the fire all year.
Poor Richard also filled the empty spaces on the calendar pages with short, witty sayings. Many of them were about work, saving, spending and the right way to use money.

Many of Poor Richard's sayings were old proverbs from different countries, which Franklin had reworded to make them sharper and shorter. Others were his own, and he was never shy about mixing the two.

Franklin liked to tease his rivals in print, and he did it with a perfectly straight face. He announced in the almanack that a competitor, Titan Leeds, would die on a day in October 1733, and he gave the hour.
Leeds wrote angrily in his own almanack that he was alive and well. Poor Richard answered that the man must be a ghost, or a fraud, and the public laughed and bought more almanacks.
The almanack sold well, perhaps as many as ten thousand copies in a year by one old estimate. Families read it aloud at the fireside, and shopkeepers repeated its sayings to their customers.
After about twenty-five years of almanacks, Franklin wrote the one for 1758 with a special plan. He gathered the best sayings into a single speech and wrapped them in a little story.
Later printers took the speech out of the almanack and printed it alone under the title The Way to Wealth. It was read in many countries, and people have quoted it ever since.
The story begins with a short preface in Richard's own voice. He says that nothing gives an author more pleasure than to find his words quoted by other learned writers.

Richard complains that other almanack makers have rarely praised him, although he has written one every year for a quarter of a century. If his books did not bring in a solid dinner, he says, he would be discouraged.

Richard decides that ordinary people are the best judges of his work, since they buy it. On his journeys he has often heard a stranger repeat one of his sayings and add the words, as Poor Richard says.
Richard admits that he has encouraged the habit himself. To make people remember and repeat wise sayings, he says, he has sometimes quoted himself with great seriousness.

Then Richard tells his readers how pleased he was by something that happened recently. He stopped his horse at a vendue, which was a public sale of merchants' goods, where a great number of people had gathered.
At a vendue, goods are laid out and people bid for them, and the sale starts at a fixed hour. That hour had not yet come, so the crowd stood about and talked about the badness of the times.
In the 1750s the colonies were at war with France and its allies, and war costs a great deal of money. Many people felt that taxes and prices were rising faster than their wages.
In the crowd stood a plain, clean old man with white hair. The people called him Father Abraham, a name that suggests a wise and gentle elder.
One man called out to the old man and asked what he thought of the times. Would the heavy taxes ruin the country, he wanted to know, and how would they ever be able to pay them?
Father Abraham stood up and replied that he would give his advice in a few words. A word to the wise is enough, he said, and many words will not fill a bushel.

Father Abraham began by agreeing with the people who were gathered around him. The taxes were indeed very heavy, he said, and if the government's taxes were the only ones, they might be much easier to pay.
But we pay many other taxes, he said, and some of them are much worse. We are taxed twice as much by our idleness, three times as much by our pride and four times as much by our folly.
The officials who collect the public taxes cannot ease these ones, Father Abraham said. There is no office where a man can go to ask for a reduction, because the only person to blame is himself.
Still, said Father Abraham, they should listen to good advice, and something might be done for them. God helps those who help themselves, he said, as Poor Richard says.
Picture two neighbours in a hard year, said Father Abraham. One of them sits by the fire and complains about his luck, while the other goes out and mends his fence and repairs his plough.

People would think it a hard government, he said, if it took a tenth part of their time for its own service. Yet idleness takes much more than that from many of us, when we count all the hours spent doing nothing.
Sloth does more than waste our time, he added, because it brings on illness and can even shorten a man's life. In his view, the body is made to be used, as well as rested.
Sloth is like rust, said Father Abraham, because it eats away a man faster than hard work wears him out. An iron tool left in the rain is ruined sooner than one that is used every day.
The key that is used every day stays bright and smooth, said Father Abraham. The one that lies forgotten in a drawer turns dull and is hard to turn in the lock.
Some of the listeners shifted uncomfortably, because they knew that they had wasted many days. Father Abraham saw it, and he moved on to a subject that touches everybody, which is time.
If you love life, said Father Abraham, then do not waste your time. Time is the very stuff that life is made of, and every hour spent is a small piece of life that is gone.
Father Abraham pointed out that many of us spend far more time in sleep than we need. We forget, he said, that every extra hour in bed is an hour that could have been used.
The sleeping fox catches no poultry, said Father Abraham, quoting Poor Richard. A fox that lies asleep in the sun will go hungry, however clever it may be.
Then he added a grim joke from Poor Richard, which was that there will be sleeping enough in the grave. The crowd laughed, but not very loudly, because the joke had a sharp edge to it.

If time is the most precious of all things, said Father Abraham, then wasting time must be the greatest waste there is. A man who throws away an hour has thrown away something that no money can buy back.
Lost time is never found again, said Father Abraham, and he said it slowly so that everyone could hear. A lost coin may turn up under a chair, but a lost hour will not.
What we call time enough always proves to be too little, said Father Abraham. The man who says he has plenty of time is often the man who is still working at midnight.
Let us be up and doing, said Father Abraham, and let us do something useful. By steady work, he said, we shall get more done and have less trouble with it.
Sloth makes everything difficult, said Father Abraham, but industry makes everything easy. The same job that frightens a lazy man seems small to a man who has already started it.
He that rises late, said Father Abraham, must trot all day and will hardly catch up with his business by night. Laziness travels so slowly, in his words, that poverty soon overtakes it on the road.
Drive your business, said Father Abraham, and do not let your business drive you. Early to bed and early to rise, he added, makes a man healthy, wealthy and wise.
Some people say that they are only waiting for better times, said Father Abraham. What is the use of hoping, he asked, when we can make the times better by getting busy ourselves?
Industry need not wish, said Father Abraham, and he that lives on hope will die fasting. In plain words, a man who only hopes for dinner will go without it.
There are no gains without pains, said Father Abraham, so we must use our own hands. Poor Richard jokes that he has no land, or if he has, it is heavily taxed.
He that has a trade has an estate, said Father Abraham. A skill that people will pay for is worth as much as a piece of land, and no tax collector can take it.
He that has a calling, said Father Abraham, has an office of profit and honour. But the trade must be worked at, and the calling must be followed well, or neither will help us pay our taxes.
If we are industrious, said Father Abraham, we shall never starve. At the working man's house, hunger looks in at the window but does not dare to come inside.

Nor will the bailiff or the constable enter such a house, he said, because industry pays debts, while despair only makes them bigger. A man who keeps working has hope, and a man who gives up has none.
You may not have found a treasure, said Father Abraham, and no rich relation may have left you money. But diligence is the mother of good luck, and God gives all things to industry.
Plough deep while sluggards sleep, said Father Abraham, and you will have corn to sell and to keep. The man who works while the lazy rest will have more than enough.
Work while it is still called today, said Father Abraham, because you do not know what may hinder you tomorrow. A rainstorm, a sickness or a visitor may be waiting at the door.
One today is worth two tomorrows, said Father Abraham. A job done now is finished, but a job put off must still be faced, and it will usually be harder.
If you have something to do tomorrow, said Father Abraham, then do it today. He did not mean that anyone must work without rest, only that the habit of delay is a dangerous one.
Suppose that you were a servant in a good man's house, said Father Abraham. Would you not be ashamed if a good master caught you doing nothing, when there was plenty of work to be done?
But you are your own master, said Father Abraham, so be ashamed to catch yourself idle. There is so much to be done for yourself, for your family and for your country.
Handle your tools without mittens, said Father Abraham, and remember that the cat in gloves catches no mice. If you want the job done, he said, you must be willing to get your hands dirty.
It is true that there is much to be done, said Father Abraham, and you may feel weak and tired. But stick to the work steadily, because constant dropping wears away stones.
By diligence and patience, said Father Abraham, the mouse ate in two the great cable. A very small animal, working quietly for long enough, can cut through a rope that a man could not break.
Little strokes fell great oaks, said Father Abraham, which is a lesson that every woodcutter knows. No one cuts a tree down with a single blow, but with a thousand small ones.
Some of the listeners asked whether a man should never rest. Father Abraham answered with Poor Richard's advice: use your time well if you wish to gain leisure, and never waste an hour.
Leisure, said Father Abraham, is time for doing something useful. The diligent man will get plenty of it, but the lazy man never will, because he has not earned a moment of it.
A life of leisure and a life of laziness are two very different things, said Father Abraham. The first is a reward that has been earned, and the second is a habit that has been allowed to grow.
Many people, said Father Abraham, would like to live by their wits alone, without any labour. But they fail in the end, because they have nothing to start with and nothing to fall back on.
Fly pleasures and they will follow you, said Father Abraham. In other words, the man who runs after fun usually fails to catch it, while the man who keeps busy finds pleasure walking behind him.
The diligent spinner has a large shift, said Father Abraham. A shift was a woman's linen undergarment, so he meant that the busy spinner always has plenty of cloth.
Now that I have a sheep and a cow, runs the saying, everybody bids me good morning. Father Abraham added that people are quick to greet a man who has something to show for his work.
But industry is not enough on its own, said Father Abraham. We must also be steady, settled and careful, and look after our own affairs with our own eyes instead of trusting too much to others.
Poor Richard says that a tree that is often moved, or a family that moves often, never grows as well as one that settles. Roots, in other words, need time to take hold.
Three removes are as bad as a fire, said Father Abraham. Each time a family moves, it loses furniture, time and money, just as it would if a fire had burned some of its belongings.
Keep your shop, said Father Abraham, and your shop will keep you. The man who looks after his work every day will find that his work looks after him in return.
If you would have your business done, said Father Abraham, go yourself, and if you do not care how it turns out, send someone else. A job that matters should be looked at by the person it matters to.
He that would thrive by the plough, said Father Abraham, must either hold the plough himself or drive the team. A farmer who sits at home while others work his field should expect a thin crop.
The eye of a master will do more work than both his hands, said Father Abraham. Workers are more careful when the owner is watching, and the owner notices problems before they grow.
Want of care does us more damage than want of knowledge, said Father Abraham. A careful man who knows a little will often do better than a clever man who does not pay attention.
Not to oversee workmen, said Father Abraham, is to leave them your purse open. A worker who is never checked may waste materials or time without meaning any harm.
Trusting too much to other people's care is the ruin of many, said Father Abraham. In the business of this world, he said, a careful doubt will protect a man better than blind trust.
A man's own care is profitable, said Father Abraham. If you would have a faithful servant, and one that you like, he said, serve yourself.
A little neglect may breed great mischief, said Father Abraham, and he gave an example in the form of a rhyme. The rhyme tells how one small nail was missing from a horseshoe.
For want of a nail the shoe was lost, he said, and for want of the shoe the horse was lost. For want of the horse the rider was lost, and all because of one small piece of iron.
So much for industry, my friends, said Father Abraham, and for attention to your own business. But we must add frugality to it, he said, if we wish our industry to be certainly successful.
A man who does not know how to save what he earns, said Father Abraham, may keep his nose to the grindstone all his life. In the end he may die without a single groat to his name.
A fat kitchen makes a lean will, said Father Abraham. The family that eats and drinks too well today will have very little to leave to the children tomorrow.
Many estates are spent in the getting, said Father Abraham, which means that people spend their money almost as soon as they have earned it. They do not think of keeping any for later.
He said that women had given up spinning and knitting for tea, and that men had given up splitting wood for punch. The pleasures cost money, and the work they replaced would have earned some.
If you would be wealthy, said Father Abraham, think of saving as well as of getting. Making money is only half of the task, and keeping some of it is the other half.

The gold of the Indies did not make Spain rich, said Father Abraham, because she spent more than she received. The Spanish government went bankrupt more than once, even though treasure ships kept arriving.
Away with your expensive follies, said Father Abraham, and you will have less reason to complain about hard times and heavy taxes. Many of our troubles, he said, are of our own making.
Wine, gambling and cheating, said Father Abraham, make the wealth small and the want great. These habits take money out of the purse, and they often take trust out of a man's reputation too.
What maintains one vice, said Father Abraham, would bring up two children. He meant that a costly bad habit can eat up the money that a family needs for food and clothes.
You may think, said Father Abraham, that a little tea, a little punch or finer clothes now and then can be no great matter. But he did not agree with that, and he said so at once.
Many a little makes a mickle, said Father Abraham. Mickle is an old word for a large amount, so he meant that small sums, repeated often, add up to a great deal.
Beware of little expenses, said Father Abraham, because a small leak will sink a great ship. A sailor knows that the biggest danger is often the one that nobody notices.
Who dainties love shall beggars prove, said Father Abraham, which means that people who love rich treats may end up with nothing. A taste for luxury is an expensive habit to keep.
Fools make feasts, said Father Abraham, and wise men eat them. The man who pays for the great dinner is out of pocket, he said, while the guest who attends it has lost nothing.

Here at this very sale, said Father Abraham, you have all come together to buy fineries and knick-knacks. You call them goods, he said, but if you do not take care they will prove to be evils to some of you.

You expect that these goods will be sold cheap, said Father Abraham, and perhaps they will be sold for less than they cost. But if you have no need of them, he said, they are dear to you at any price.
Buy what you have no need of, said Father Abraham, and before long you will have to sell the things that you do need. A man who fills his house with extras may soon find that he has sold his bed.
At a great pennyworth, said Father Abraham, pause a while. A pennyworth is a bargain, and he meant that the cheapness may not be real, or that it may leave you short.
Many have been ruined by buying good pennyworths, said Father Abraham, as Poor Richard says. The danger is not the price, he said, but the way a bargain tempts us to spend more.
It is foolish to lay out money in a purchase of repentance, said Father Abraham. This is done every day at sales like this one, he said, for want of minding the almanack.
Many a one, said Father Abraham, has gone with a hungry belly for the sake of fine clothes on his back. Some have even half-starved their families to pay for a show of wealth.
Silks and satins, scarlet and velvet, said Father Abraham, put out the kitchen fire. In other words, money spent on rich cloth is money that is no longer buying wood and food.
These things are not necessaries, said Father Abraham, and they can hardly be called conveniences. Yet because they look pretty, he said, how many people want to have them!
In this way, said Father Abraham, the artificial wants of mankind become more numerous than the natural ones. Food, warmth and shelter are few, but the things we think we want are endless.
For one poor person there are a hundred indigent, said Father Abraham. He meant that the wants we invent make a great many people feel poor who need not be.
By such extravagance, said Father Abraham, the genteel are brought down to poverty. They are forced to borrow from people they once looked down on, who kept their place through industry and thrift.
A ploughman on his legs, said Father Abraham, is higher than a gentleman on his knees. The independent working man stands taller than a rich man who has to beg.

Perhaps they had a small estate left to them, said Father Abraham, which they never worked to earn. They think it will always be day and never night, and that a little spent out of so much is not worth minding.
Always taking out of the meal tub and never putting in, said Father Abraham, soon comes to the bottom. A fortune that is only spent, and never added to, will run out sooner than anyone expects.
When the well is dry, said Father Abraham, they know the worth of water. People often value a thing only after they have lost it, and by then it may be too late.
If you would know the value of money, said Father Abraham, go and try to borrow some. You will soon find out how hard it is to come by and how much it costs.
He that goes a-borrowing goes a-sorrowing, said Father Abraham, and so does the lender who must go and collect the money. A loan can bring a great deal of trouble to both sides of the bargain.
Poor Dick, as Father Abraham called him, says that fond pride of dress is sure a very curse. Before you consult your fancy, says the rhyme, consult your purse.
Pride is as loud a beggar as want, said Father Abraham, and a great deal more saucy. A man who is poor from need asks politely, but a man who is poor from pride demands as if it were his right.
When you have bought one fine thing, said Father Abraham, you must buy ten more to match it. One new hat makes the old coat and the old shoes look shabby.
It is easier to suppress the first desire, said Poor Dick, than to satisfy all the desires that follow it. If you refuse the first temptation, you save yourself from all the rest.
It is as foolish for the poor to copy the rich as for a frog to swell up to equal an ox. In the old fable, the frog only hurts itself.
Large vessels may venture more, said Father Abraham, but little boats should keep near the shore. A rich man can take a risk that would drown a poor one.
The folly is soon punished, said Father Abraham, for pride that dines on vanity sups on contempt. A person who shows off at midday may find that nobody respects him by evening.
In another place, said Father Abraham, Poor Richard says that pride breakfasted with Plenty, dined with Poverty and supped with Infamy. The proud man's day begins in abundance and ends in disgrace.
After all, asked Father Abraham, what is the use of this pride of appearance, for which so much is risked and so much is suffered? He wanted them to think about what they were really buying.
It cannot promote health, said Father Abraham, and it cannot ease pain. A man in a silk coat has the same fever as a man in an old one.
It does not make a person any better, said Father Abraham, but it does create envy and it hastens misfortune. The neighbours who see a showy man are often not pleased for him.
But what madness it must be, said Father Abraham, to run in debt for such things! He meant luxuries and showy extras that nobody really needs.
The terms of this sale offer six months' credit, said Father Abraham. That has perhaps tempted some of you to come, because you cannot spare ready money and hope to be fine without it.
Think what you do when you run in debt, said Father Abraham. You give another person power over your liberty, and he may take it up whenever he likes.
If you cannot pay at the time, said Father Abraham, you will be ashamed to see your creditor. You will be afraid whenever you speak to him, and you will cross the street to avoid him.
You will make poor, pitiful excuses, said Father Abraham, and by degrees you will lose your honesty. At last you may sink into plain and shameless lying.
The second vice is lying, says Poor Richard, and the first is running in debt. Father Abraham said that the two usually walk together, one behind the other.
Lying rides upon debt's back, said Father Abraham, and a free person should never be ashamed or afraid to look anyone in the face. He said that this is worth more than any fine coat.
Poverty often takes away a man's spirit and his good qualities, said Father Abraham. It is hard for an empty bag to stand upright, as Poor Richard truly says.
Imagine a prince who forbade you to dress like a gentleman, said Father Abraham, on pain of prison. Would you not call that government a tyranny, and would you not complain very loudly?
And yet, said Father Abraham, you are about to put yourself under that very tyranny when you run in debt for fine clothes. You would fight the law, he said, but you will sign the paper.
In those days, said Father Abraham, a creditor could have the debtor locked up in gaol for a long time. In some cases he could even sell him to work as a servant if he could not pay.
When you have got your bargain, said Father Abraham, you may not think much about paying. But creditors, as Poor Richard tells us, have better memories than debtors.
In another place, said Father Abraham, Poor Richard says that creditors are a superstitious sect. They are great observers of set days and times, and they never miss one.
The day comes round before you are aware, said Father Abraham, and the demand is made before you are ready to meet it. A debt seems far away on the day when it is signed.
Or if you remember your debt, said Father Abraham, the time that seemed so long at first will seem very short as it runs out. Time seems to grow wings on his heels as well as on his shoulders.
Those have a short Lent, says Poor Richard, who owe money to be paid at Easter. Lent is forty days of fasting before Easter, and for a debtor those days pass very fast.

The borrower is a slave to the lender, said Father Abraham, and the debtor is a slave to the creditor. So disdain the chain, he said, preserve your freedom and be industrious and free, frugal and free.
Perhaps you think you are doing well at present, said Father Abraham, and that you can afford a little extra spending. He looked around the crowd as though he could see every purse in it.
But for old age and hard times, save while you can, said Father Abraham. No morning sun lasts a whole day, and a good year can be followed by a bad one.
Your gains may be small and uncertain, said Father Abraham, but your expenses will go on as long as you live. The harvest may fail, but the family still has to eat.
It is easier to build two chimneys, said Father Abraham, than to keep one of them supplied with wood. A big house costs less to put up than it costs to run.
So it is better to go to bed without supper, said Father Abraham, than to get up in debt. A hungry night is soon over, but a debt is still there in the morning.
Keep an account of what you earn and what you spend, said Father Abraham, and look at it often. A leak can only be mended by someone who knows where it is.
Even a few pennies put aside every week will grow into a useful sum, said Father Abraham. Nobody has to save a fortune in one day; they only have to start.
Get what you can, said Father Abraham, and hold on to what you get. That, as Poor Richard says, is the stone that will turn all your lead into gold.
Long ago, men called alchemists hoped to find a magic stone that would turn lead into gold. For hundreds of years they tried, and not one of them ever succeeded.
The real philosopher's stone, said Father Abraham, is a habit of working and saving. Once you have it, you will no longer complain of bad times or of the trouble of paying taxes.
This doctrine, my friends, is reason and wisdom, said Father Abraham. Then his voice grew softer, and the people leaned in to hear what came next.
But after all, said Father Abraham, do not depend too much on your own industry, thrift and good sense. They are excellent things, but they are not everything.
They can all be blasted, said Father Abraham, without the blessing of Heaven. A hailstorm can flatten a field, and a fire can destroy a shop in one night.
Therefore, said Father Abraham, ask for that blessing humbly. In his day, as in ours, many people felt that it was wise to admit that they could not control everything.
The rich merchants and the poor farmers stood side by side in the crowd, and for a moment they all listened as one. The old man had not spoken of rank, only of what could happen to anyone.
And be not uncharitable, said Father Abraham, to those who seem to lack that blessing. Comfort them, and help them if you can, for you may need help yourself one day.
Not everyone who is poor has become poor through folly. Sickness, bad harvests and war can ruin careful people too, and they deserve our help.
Remember that Job suffered, said Father Abraham, and was afterwards prosperous. Job is a man in the Bible who lost his wealth and his health, and later received good things again.
Franklin tried hard to live by this lesson in his own city of Philadelphia. In 1736 he helped to start a volunteer fire company in Philadelphia, where neighbours promised to help one another.
In 1751 Franklin helped to found a hospital in Philadelphia, the Pennsylvania Hospital. It was meant to care for sick people, including those who were too poor to pay.
And now to conclude, said Father Abraham, experience keeps a dear school. Fools will learn in no other, and hardly even in that one.
A dear school is an expensive school, and in this one every mistake costs real money. The lessons of experience are paid for with losses, and the fees are never cheap.
The cheapest lessons are the ones we learn from other people's mistakes. Look around you before you pay for a lesson of your own.
We may give advice, said Father Abraham, but we cannot give conduct. Giving a person a good rule is easy, but nobody can live by it for him.
Knowing what to do is very different from really doing it. The best rule in the world is useless to a person who never puts it into practice.
However, remember this, said Father Abraham: they that will not be counselled cannot be helped. A doctor cannot cure a man who will not take the medicine.
And further, said Father Abraham, if you will not hear Reason, she will surely rap your knuckles. The crowd laughed, because many of them still remembered a strict teacher.
Father Abraham looked around the crowd with a kind smile. He had spoken sharply at times, but everyone could see that he wished them well.
He had said everything that he wanted to say, and he thanked the people for their attention. Then he stepped back, put his hat on again and was silent.
For a moment the whole crowd was quiet and still. Everyone had been given a great deal to think about, and nobody wanted to speak first.
So the old man ended his speech, and Richard Saunders watched from his horse. Slowly the crowd began to stir and to break up into little groups.
The people had heard the speech and approved of the doctrine. Many of them told each other that every word of it was exactly right.
And yet they immediately practised the contrary, just as if it had been a common sermon. Not one of them seemed to remember a single word.
For the vendue opened at that very moment, and the people began to buy extravagantly. Hands went up all over the square, and the bidding grew louder and louder.
A gilded looking glass, a length of silk and a set of fine cups were all sold in the first hour. Many of the buyers could hardly afford the prices they had agreed to pay.
Richard Saunders sat on his horse and thought about what he had just heard. He found that the good old man had thoroughly studied his almanacks.
Richard recognised sayings that he had scattered through the almanack over twenty-five years. Now they were all gathered together and repeated in the old man's own words.
Richard was pleased to hear his sayings so well repeated. As he had once written, nothing pleases an author more than to find his work respectfully quoted.
Richard did not let his pride carry him away. He resolved to be the better for the echo of his own sayings.
He had meant to buy cloth that day for a new coat. Instead he went home and decided to wear his old coat a little longer.
Richard ended his preface the way he always did, by signing himself the reader's servant. Behind that friendly name stood Benjamin Franklin, who was smiling at his own joke.
The speech first appeared in the almanack for the year 1758, and many people read it. It was so popular that printers soon began to print it by itself, as a small book and on single large sheets.
In 1757 Franklin sailed across the ocean to London, where he was to speak for Pennsylvania. He spent many of the following years living in England.
By then his experiments with electricity had made him famous in Europe. He had also invented the lightning rod, which protects buildings from lightning.
In 1776 Franklin was one of the men who signed the Declaration of Independence. Later that year he sailed to France to ask the French for help.
In the 1770s French readers could enjoy his sayings in their own language. They were printed in a book called La Science du Bonhomme Richard, which means The Science of Good Man Richard.
In 1779 an American naval officer, John Paul Jones, named his warship Bonhomme Richard. He chose the name to honour Franklin and the French name for Poor Richard.
In 1783 Franklin was one of the Americans who made peace with Britain, in the Treaty of Paris. Two years later, in 1785, he sailed back to Philadelphia.
Franklin died in Philadelphia on 17 April 1790, at the age of eighty-four. He left behind his Autobiography, the story of his life, which he never finished.
More than two hundred years later, the message of The Way to Wealth is still simple. Work hard, spend carefully, stay out of debt, and keep a little for the days ahead.
C1C2: Benjamin Franklin was a printer in Philadelphia, and his shop smelled of ink, paper and lamp oil from early morning until late at night. He was also a writer, an inventor and, in time, one of the men who helped to found his country. Yet one of the humblest things he made each year was a small, cheap book that found its way into thousands of homes.

Benjamin was born in Boston in 1706 into a household so crowded that his father, Josiah, had seventeen children in all. Josiah made soap and candles for a living, and the house must have smelled of hot fat from morning to night. There was never much money to spare, which was a lesson the boy learned long before he wrote a word about it.

Benjamin had only about two years of schooling, since his father could not afford more and wanted his help in the family trade. The boy made up for it by devouring every volume he could borrow, and he often sat up half the night over a book by candlelight. It was the first sign that his true education would be the one that he gave himself.

At the age of twelve Benjamin was apprenticed to his older brother James, who ran a printing shop in Boston, and he agreed to serve him for many years. He learned to set tiny metal letters into rows, to rub ink over them and to pull the heavy press until a clean page came out. The work was hard on the hands, but the shop was also full of words, and he never tired of them.

At about the age of sixteen Benjamin began writing funny letters for his brother's newspaper, and he signed them with the made-up name of a widow called Silence Dogood. He slipped each one under the printing-house door at night, so that James would judge the writing on its merits. The letters were a great success, and James printed them without any idea that the clever widow was his own young apprentice.

The brothers quarrelled often, and since James had a hot temper and sometimes struck him, Benjamin decided he had had enough. In 1723, at the age of seventeen, he left Boston quietly by boat with very little money in his pocket. His destination was Philadelphia, a city where nobody knew him and where he would have to prove himself from the beginning.

Franklin reached Philadelphia on a Sunday morning in October, tired, dirty and almost without money in his pocket. He wrote many years later that he bought three large rolls of bread and walked up the street with one under each arm while he ate the third. It is an odd picture of a man who would one day dine with kings, and he plainly enjoyed telling the tale.

Franklin soon found work with a printer in Philadelphia, and he gained a name as one of the hardest workers in the town. Within a few years, helped by friends who lent him money and trusted his character, he was able to open a printing house of his own. From that day on, the shop that carried his name had to earn its keep, and he never forgot it.

In 1727 Franklin gathered a small group of ambitious friends into a club that he called the Junto, and its members met once a week to discuss questions of morals, politics and science. They also helped one another's businesses, passing on customers, books and useful advice whenever one of them had more than he needed. Many of the schemes that later improved Philadelphia were first debated around their crowded table.

In 1729 Franklin took over a newspaper, the Pennsylvania Gazette, and made it lively enough that people looked forward to every issue. Two years later he and his friends began the Library Company, in which each member paid a small fee so that all could borrow books that none could have bought alone. By the early 1730s he was one of the busiest and best-known printers in the city, and he was looking for a new project.

In December 1732 Franklin printed the first Poor Richard's Almanack, a book meant to be used throughout the year 1733. He did not put his own name on the title page; he gave the credit to a made-up writer called Richard Saunders. The disguise let him joke, boast and complain in a voice that was not quite his own.

Franklin borrowed the name Richard Saunders from an English almanack maker who had lived in the century before him. His own Richard was a poor and cheerful student of the stars, with a wife named Bridget who thought that his hobby ought to bring in some money. Readers loved the pair, for they were funny, a little shabby and recognisable to anyone who had ever struggled to pay a bill.

An almanack in those days was a yearly book that held a calendar, the phases of the moon, tide tables, guesses about the weather and a few useful facts for farmers and families. Most households owned one, and some owned hardly any other book apart from the Bible. The book was therefore read, reread and nailed to a wall, which made it the perfect place for a clever writer to say something.

Poor Richard filled the empty corners of the calendar pages with short, witty sayings, which a reader might find while looking up the date of the next full moon. Many of them concerned work, thrift, honesty and the proper use of money, and they were written to be remembered. Each one was so brief that a man could repeat it to his neighbour at the gate.

Many of Poor Richard's sayings were old proverbs gathered from many lands and periods, which Franklin reworded until they were sharper, shorter and easier to remember. Others he made up himself, and he did not trouble to tell his readers which were which. What mattered to him was that a good thought should be passed on in its best possible form.

Franklin enjoyed a good quarrel, and he picked one with a rival almanack maker named Titan Leeds. As a joke, Poor Richard announced that Leeds would die on a particular day in October 1733, and he even named the hour with a straight face. The prediction was outrageous, and everyone who read it knew that it was meant to make them smile.

Leeds replied in his own almanack that he was alive and well, and he was furious. Poor Richard calmly answered that a dead man could hardly be expected to admit his condition, and that the angry writer must be a fraud or perhaps a ghost. The whole dispute was good-natured fun on one side, and it made the name of Poor Richard famous.

The almanack sold extremely well, with as many as ten thousand copies in a good year by one old estimate, which was a remarkable figure in a land of scattered farms and small towns. Families read it aloud by the fire, and shopkeepers and farmers repeated its sayings to anyone who would listen. In short, Poor Richard had become a voice that was heard in almost every household.

After about twenty-five years of almanacks, Franklin did something clever with the one for the year 1758. He gathered the best of the sayings into a single speech, and he wrapped that speech in a short story so that the advice would arrive in the mouth of a character. It was a neat way to turn a pile of proverbs into one long argument.

In later years printers took the speech out of the almanack, published it alone and gave it the title The Way to Wealth. It was reprinted many times and translated into other languages, and people who have never opened it still quote its lines. The little story that follows is the one that carried those lines so far.

The story begins with a short preface written in the voice of Poor Richard himself. Nothing delights an author more, he declares, than to find his words respectfully quoted by other learned writers. It is a pleasure, he adds with a knowing wink, that he has known only very seldom in all his years of writing.

Richard complains that the other almanack makers have rarely said a kind word about him, although he has been writing for a full quarter of a century. If his books did not bring him some solid pudding, he admits, the lack of praise would have discouraged him altogether. Franklin, of course, is poking fun at the vanity of authors, and at his own in particular.

Richard concludes that ordinary people are the best judges of his work, since they are willing to buy it with their own money. On his rambles, in places where nobody knows his face, he has often heard a stranger quote one of his sayings and finish with the words, as Poor Richard says. That, he feels, is a satisfaction worth more to a humble writer than all the praise of rival authors.

Richard confesses that he has encouraged the habit himself, and in a rather shameless way. To persuade people to remember and repeat his wise sentences, he says, he has sometimes quoted himself with the greatest gravity. This sort of joke, in which the author laughs at his own pride, was part of the charm of the whole almanack.

Then Richard tells his readers how greatly he was gratified by something that happened to him recently. He stopped his horse beside a vendue, which was a public sale of merchants' goods, where a great number of people had gathered in the open air. Judge for yourselves, he says, how much the little incident that followed must have pleased him.

At a vendue the goods are laid out on tables or on the ground, and the buyers bid against one another until each article is sold to the highest offer. The hour of the sale had not yet come, so the crowd stood about in little groups and talked about the badness of the times. As people have always done, they found that it was easy to complain and hard to say what could be done.

The 1750s were an anxious time in the colonies, which were at war with France and its allies, and war is always an expensive business. Taxes were heavy and prices were rising, so many families felt that their money could not stretch as far as it used to. It is no wonder that the crowd at the sale could talk of nothing else.

Among the crowd stood a plain, clean old man with white hair, who listened more than he spoke. The people called him Father Abraham, and the name, which recalls the old patriarch of the Bible, suggests that they thought of him as a wise and gentle elder. Franklin never says who he really was, and perhaps he was meant to be everyone's grandfather.

One of the company called out to the old man and asked him, in the name of everyone there, what he thought of the times. Would these heavy taxes not quite ruin the country, he wanted to know, and how would anyone ever be able to pay them? He ended by begging the old man to tell them plainly what they ought to do about it all.

Father Abraham rose to his feet and replied that, if they wanted his advice, he would give it in a few words. A word to the wise is enough, he said, quoting Poor Richard, and many words will not fill a bushel. The people begged him to say what he thought, and they crowded around him to hear.

Father Abraham began by agreeing with the worried man, for he did not like to make light of anybody's troubles. The taxes were indeed very heavy, he said, and if the ones laid on by the government were the only ones that people had to pay, they might be discharged without much difficulty. He paused, and the crowd waited for the word that they knew was coming.

But we have many other taxes to pay, he went on, and some of them are far more grievous than those of the government. We are taxed twice as much by our idleness, three times as much by our pride and four times as much by our folly. The collectors of these taxes never knock at the door, he implied, because we carry the money to them ourselves.

The officials who collect the public taxes can do nothing to lighten these private ones, the old man said, for there is no office to which a man can carry a complaint. Nobody can ask for a reduction of the tax that he lays upon himself, and no government is able to forgive it. In that sense the burden was a heavier one, but it was also one that each person could lift.

Still, said Father Abraham, they might listen to some good advice, and then something could be done to help them. God helps those who help themselves, he reminded them, as Poor Richard says, and the proverb was already old when Franklin gave it a place in his almanack. He meant it in the plain sense that Heaven rewards effort and does not reward complaining.

Picture two neighbours in the same hard year, the old man invited them, each with the same weather, the same taxes and the same worries. One of them sits by his fire complaining about his luck, while the other goes out, mends his fence, repairs his plough and looks for something that he can sell. Which of the two, he asked, would they expect to be in better spirits by the spring?

It would be thought a hard government that took one tenth part of a man's time for its own service, Father Abraham observed, and every farmer in the crowd would complain of it. Yet idleness takes much more than a tenth from many of us, if we count all the hours spent in doing nothing and all the hours spent in amusements that come to nothing. We grumble at the tax collector, but we pay the lazy tax without a murmur.

Sloth does more than waste our time, the old man added, for it brings on diseases and so shortens life itself. In his day nobody could give a scientific explanation, but ordinary experience seemed to show that the body, like a road, is kept in good repair by being used. Modern doctors would say that regular activity is indeed good for health, though they would also insist that rest has its place.

Sloth, like rust, consumes faster than labour wears, the old man said, and the farmers who heard him could picture the pitted blade of an iron tool left out in the rain. A plough that is used every day gets worn at the edge, but one that is left alone in the damp is eaten through. People are in the same case, he suggested, and they decay when their gifts are never put to work.

The key that is used every day stays bright, Father Abraham said, because the touch of many hands keeps it polished. The key that lies forgotten in a drawer turns dull and stiff, and when the day comes that it is needed, it may hardly turn in the lock.
