He wanted his listeners to see that a mind and a pair of hands behave in the same way.

Some of the listeners shifted uncomfortably, for they knew very well that they had wasted many days and could not honestly call themselves busy. Father Abraham noticed their faces, and he did not scold them, but moved gently on to a subject that touches every person alive. That subject was time, which the rich and the poor receive in exactly the same measure.

If you love life, said Father Abraham, then do not squander time, for time is the very stuff that life is made of. A man may lose a purse and then earn another, but every hour that he throws away is taken from the only account that he can never refill. The crowd was quiet now, because that was a bill that every person present could understand and none could argue with.

How much more time than is necessary we spend in sleep, Father Abraham remarked, and how seldom we stop to count the cost. Every extra hour in bed is an hour that might have been used for something, and in a farming life with long days of labour, the early light was too good to waste. A modern reader should add that enough sleep is itself essential to health, and the old man would surely agree.

The sleeping fox catches no poultry, said Father Abraham, borrowing the line from Poor Richard, and the farmers who kept hens understood the joke at once. A fox may be as clever as a man, but if it lies in the sun while the hens are awake, it will go hungry all the same. Cleverness alone, in other words, has never yet put a single meal on anybody's table.

Then he added a grim joke that he had borrowed from Poor Richard, which was that there will be sleeping enough in the grave. The crowd laughed, though not very loudly, for the joke had a sharp edge on it. The point was that we have only so many waking hours, and a wise person spends them while they last.

If time be of all things the most precious, said Father Abraham, then wasting time must be the greatest extravagance of all. A spendthrift may lose his gold and later earn it back, but a man who throws away an hour has thrown away something that no money can buy. By that measure, he suggested, most of us are much richer in coins than in minutes and much poorer than we think.

Lost time is never found again, said Father Abraham, and he said it slowly so that every person could hear. A lost coin may roll out from under a chair, and a lost glove may turn up in a drawer, but an hour that has been wasted never returns to the owner. He let the words hang in the air for a moment, and nobody in the crowd spoke, before he went on.

What we call time enough, Father Abraham warned them, always proves to be little enough in the end. The man who says he has plenty of time is usually the man who is still struggling with his work when the light has failed and the market has closed. Delay is a quiet thief, he said, because it never seems to take anything until the moment when everything has gone.

Let us then be up and doing, Father Abraham told the crowd, and let us do it to the purpose, so that by diligence we may achieve more with less perplexity. Busy hands that have no plan, he explained, do not accomplish much, but busy hands that are guided by a clear aim can do wonders. It was, he said, as plain as the difference between a river that is led through a mill and one that merely floods the field.

Sloth makes all things difficult, said Father Abraham, but industry makes all things easy, and he gave the crowd a moment to turn the idea over. The same task that frightens a lazy man into delay seems small to a man who has already rolled up his sleeves and begun. Most of the weight, he implied, is found in the dreading of the work and not in the lifting.

He that rises late, said Father Abraham, must trot all day and will scarcely overtake his business at night. Laziness, he went on, travels so slowly that poverty soon catches up with it, just as a hungry dog catches up with a man who is dragging his feet. The laughter in the crowd this time was warmer and easier, because the listeners recognised themselves in the picture.

Drive your business, said Father Abraham, so that it does not end by driving you, for the man who is pulled along by his tasks has already lost the reins. Then he recited the famous rule of Poor Richard, which says that early to bed and early to rise makes a man healthy, wealthy and wise. Whether it always works is a fair question, but the habit of planning the day certainly did the old farmers no harm.

Some of you, Father Abraham said, seem to be waiting for better times, as if the times were a cart that might arrive at the door by itself. What is the use of hoping, he asked, when we may make the times better if only we bestir ourselves? He did not deny that hard seasons come, but he refused to let anyone sit down and wait for luck.

Industry need not wish, said Father Abraham, for the hard worker is already busy making what he wants, and he that lives upon hope will die fasting. In plain words, the man who only hopes for his dinner will probably go to bed without it. Wishing costs nothing, he observed, which is exactly the reason why it is worth so very little to anyone.

There are no gains without pains, Father Abraham told them, and he added a rhyme in which Poor Richard calls on his two helping hands, since he has no lands, or if he has any, they are smartly taxed. It was a way of saying that nobody had a right to wait for an inheritance. The one property that every man owns, however poor he may be, is his own capacity to do a day's work.

He that has a trade, said Father Abraham, has an estate, and the shoemaker, the carpenter and the weaver in the crowd nodded as they heard it. A skill that people will pay for is worth as much as a farm, and it cannot easily be sold off, lost at cards or seized by a creditor. The man who carries his fortune in his two hands is, in a sense, never poor.

He that has a calling, the old man said, has an office of profit and honour, and in that sense a good tailor is as much a public servant as a magistrate. But the trade must be worked at and the calling well followed, he warned, or neither the estate nor the office will help us to pay our taxes. A skill that is never used is only a pleasant story about what one might have been.

If we are industrious, said Father Abraham, we shall never starve, and he painted a picture for them. At the working man's house, he said, hunger looks in at the window but never dares to enter, as a stray dog may stand at the gate and watch a family eat without daring to cross the yard. It was a comforting thought for people who had been worrying about empty larders.

Nor will the bailiff or the constable enter such a house, he went on, since industry pays debts, while despair only increases them. The man who keeps working can look at a small debt and see how it may be paid in time, but the man who has given up sees only a mountain. The difference between the two is not always in their circumstances; it is often in their courage.

What though you have found no treasure, said Father Abraham, and no rich relation has left you a legacy? Diligence, he told them, is the mother of good luck, and God gives all things to industry, which is another way of saying that luck comes more often to the people who are out in the field to meet it. The listeners who had been waiting for an uncle to die looked a little embarrassed.

Plough deep while sluggards sleep, said Father Abraham, quoting a line of Poor Richard that rhymed as neatly as a nursery verse, and you shall have corn to sell and to keep. The farmer who is working his field before sunrise will have a crop to market in the autumn and a store of grain for the winter. The sleeper, on the other hand, will have nothing in the barn when the cold weather comes except his pleasant dreams.

Work while it is called today, said Father Abraham, for you cannot tell how much you may be hindered tomorrow. A storm may break, a horse may go lame, a child may fall ill or a neighbour may arrive with a long and tiresome story. The man who has done his work in good time is the only one who can face such interruptions calmly.

One today is worth two tomorrows, said Father Abraham, and he pointed out that the arithmetic was easy to check. A job done now is finished and forgotten, but a job put off must still be faced later, and it has usually grown while it waited. Every tired person in the crowd could name a task that had behaved in exactly that way.

If you have something to do tomorrow, said Father Abraham, then do it today, and the sentence was as short as a command. He did not mean that anyone should work without rest, only that the habit of delay is a hungry one that eats a little more of a man's life every week. Once it has taken hold, he warned, it becomes easier to put things off than to do them.

Suppose that you were a servant, said Father Abraham, in the house of a good master who paid you fairly and trusted you. Would you not be ashamed if he came in and caught you idle, when you knew very well that there was work waiting to be done? Nobody in the crowd answered him aloud, but several heads were bowed and a few of the men looked at their boots.

But if you are your own master, said Father Abraham, then you should be ashamed to catch yourself idle, when there is so much to be done for yourself, for your family, for your country and for your king. In those days a man's duties spread out around him like the rings from a stone dropped into a pond. The old man asked only that each person take care of the nearest rings first.

Handle your tools without mittens, said Father Abraham, and remember that the cat in gloves catches no mice, an image that raised a smile on the faces of the farmers. If a man wishes to get a job done, he explained, he cannot be fussy about getting his hands dirty or his fingers cold. The laziest excuses, he said, are the ones that are dressed up as being careful.

It is true that there is much to be done, said Father Abraham, and some of you may be weak in the hands or short of heart. But stick to the work steadily, he urged, and you will see great results in time, for constant dropping wears away stones. Anyone who has seen a hollow worn into a doorstep by a hundred years of feet will understand the truth of it.

By diligence and patience, said Father Abraham, the mouse ate in two the cable, and his audience could easily picture the small creature gnawing through a rope that was as thick as a man's wrist. The mouse is weak and the cable is strong, but the mouse has time and an unbroken purpose on its side. The lesson, he said, was that steady persistence can beat strength, provided that it never stops for long.

Little strokes fell great oaks, said Father Abraham, and every woodcutter in the crowd knew that this was simply true. No man brings down a mighty tree with one blow, but a patient axe, swung steadily from morning until noon, will bring down the biggest trunk in the forest. A large task becomes small, he concluded, when it is cut up into a great many little strokes.

Some in the crowd murmured that a man must be allowed some rest, and Father Abraham heard them. Use your time well if you mean to gain leisure, he said, quoting Poor Richard, and since you are not sure of a minute, do not throw away an hour. The man who plans his work, he explained, is the one who finds free afternoons at the end of it.

Leisure, said Father Abraham, is time for doing something useful, and he was careful to define the word so that nobody could mistake it for idleness. The diligent man will obtain such time in plenty, because he has finished the jobs that other people are still dreading, while the lazy man will never enjoy it. Rest tastes sweetest, in his view, when there is something behind it that has been well done.

A life of leisure and a life of laziness are two very different things, said Father Abraham, and he drew the line between them as clearly as he could. The first is a reward that a man has earned by useful labour, spent perhaps on reading, on friends or on the education of his children, while the second is merely a habit that has been allowed to grow. One makes a person richer in mind, and the other makes a person poorer in every way.

Many people, said Father Abraham, would like to live by their wits alone, without any honest labour, and some of them are clever enough to make a show of it for a while. But they break, in the old phrase, for want of stock, which means that they fail in the end because they have no capital, no tools and no real trade to fall back on. A quick tongue, he said, is never a substitute for a steady hand, and sooner or later the bills arrive.

Fly pleasures and they will follow you, said Father Abraham, and the saying turns the world's common wisdom neatly on its head. The man who runs breathlessly after amusement is seldom happy for long, he suggested, while the man who is busy with good work finds that contentment walks quietly beside him. Joy, like a shy bird, comes nearest to people who are not chasing it.

The diligent spinner has a large shift, said Father Abraham, and the women in the crowd smiled because they understood the old-fashioned expression at once. A shift was a woman's long linen undergarment, so he meant that the person who spins steadily will never be short of cloth. The thread that is made patiently each evening turns into a wardrobe by the end of the year.

Now that I have a sheep and a cow, runs the old saying, everybody bids me a pleasant good morrow. Father Abraham smiled as he added that people have always been quick to tip their hats to a man who has some property, and slow to notice one who has none. The remark was a little cynical, but it was meant to show that steady work earns respect as well as bread.

But with our industry, said Father Abraham, we must likewise be steady, settled and careful, and we must oversee our own affairs with our own eyes instead of trusting too much to other people. A man who works very hard and then leaves his business to others, he warned, is like a farmer who ploughs well and then sleeps while the cattle trample his corn. Care, he concluded, is the second half of industry, and without it the first half is largely wasted.

Poor Richard says, said Father Abraham, that he never saw an oft-removed tree, nor yet an oft-removed family, that throve so well as those that settled be. A plant that is dug up every season has no chance to send its roots deep, and a family that is always moving never has a chance to make a name, a trade and a circle of friends. Stability, he implied, is itself a kind of wealth, and one that no fire or tax collector can easily take away.

Three removes are as bad as a fire, said Father Abraham, and by a remove he meant a change of house. Each time that a family moves, some furniture is broken, some goods are mislaid and a good deal of labour and money is squandered, just as if a small fire had passed through the household. This does not mean that no one should ever move, only that moving costs more than we usually count.

Keep your shop, said Father Abraham, and your shop will keep you, which was a tidy little saying that people could carry home in their heads. The man who tends his business faithfully every day, he explained, will find that the business in turn tends to him, and feeds his children as well. It is a partnership that grows slowly, he added, but it is one that very seldom turns false or fails.

If you would have your business done, said Father Abraham, then go yourself, and if you do not much care how it turns out, send somebody else. A messenger will carry your words, but he will not carry your worries, and a job that matters deserves the attention of the one person to whom it matters most. The crowd laughed, since most of them had been let down by a hired hand at some time.

He that by the plough would thrive, said Father Abraham, must either hold or drive, which meant that the owner of a farm must put his own hand to the work or stand in the field and direct it. A farmer who sits comfortably at home while hired men plough his land should expect a poor harvest and a ready excuse for it. Nothing improves a crop like the presence of the man who will eat it.

The eye of a master will do more work than both his hands, said Father Abraham, and he meant that watching is itself a form of labour. Workers are more careful when the owner is near, and the owner, for his part, notices small faults before they swell into large losses. Every shopkeeper in the crowd had learned that it is the mistake nobody saw that costs the most.

Want of care, said Father Abraham, does us more damage than want of knowledge, and he said it as a man who had known many clever fools. A careful man who knows only a little will often do better than a brilliant one who pays no attention to what he is doing. Education matters a great deal, he granted, but it can never perform the labour that only vigilance can do.

Not to oversee workmen, said Father Abraham, is to leave them your purse open, and the proverb has the sharpness of a pin. A worker who is never checked may waste materials or hours without meaning any harm, and a worker who is tempted may do worse. It is a mild kindness to everyone, he added, to keep a friendly eye on the work as it goes along.

Trusting too much to other people's care, said Father Abraham, is the ruin of many, and he put it in a rather bitter way. In the affairs of this world, he said, men are saved not by faith but by the want of it, which is to say that a little healthy doubt in matters of money protects us better than an open heart. He was talking about shops and bargains and hired hands, of course, and certainly not about friends or family.

A man's own care is profitable, said Father Abraham, and he gave them a saying that was half a joke and half a sermon. If you would have a faithful servant, and one that you like, he told the crowd, then serve yourself, for no hired person will ever take as much trouble over your affairs as you will. The laughter that followed was the sheepish kind, the kind that comes from being caught out.

A little neglect may breed great mischief, said Father Abraham, and to prove it he recited an old rhyme about a horse that lost a single nail. The rhyme is brief enough for a child to learn, but it contains a whole chain of consequences, each link following from the one before. He asked the people to listen to it with care, because the lesson was all in the order of the links.

For want of a nail the shoe was lost, the old man recited, and for want of the shoe the horse was lost, and for want of the horse the rider was lost. The rider, in the old rhyme, was overtaken by the enemy, and all because somebody had not troubled to look after a single nail. Small things, he said, should never be despised, for large troubles grow out of them.

So much for industry, my friends, said Father Abraham, and for attention to one's own business, and the crowd shifted its weight and prepared to hear the harder part. To these, he went on, we must add frugality, if we would make our industry more certainly successful. It is one thing to bring money in, he said, and quite another to keep some of it.

A man who does not know how to save as he gets, said Father Abraham, may keep his nose to the grindstone all his life, and die at last not worth a groat. A groat was a small silver coin of little value, so the picture is of a man who has worked for forty years and has nothing left to show. The crowd understood that labour without thrift is like water poured into a basket.

A fat kitchen makes a lean will, said Father Abraham, and the old saying drew a laugh as well as a sigh. The family that dines too richly every day will find that there is little left in the chest when the time comes to divide an estate. Every extravagant dinner, he suggested, is a coin that will never reach the heir.

Many estates are spent in the getting, said Father Abraham, which meant that a man could earn a large income and still end with nothing, because he spent it as quickly as it arrived. A fortune that is stopped at the front door by a good salary may slip out through the back door by way of the shop and the tavern. He urged them to watch both of the doors very carefully, and not to guard only the front one.

Franklin has the old man say that in these days women had forsaken spinning and knitting for the sake of tea, while men had put down the axe and the wedge for the sake of punch. Both luxuries cost money, and the work that had been dropped to make room for them would have earned some. It was a sharp, rather unfair complaint, but it showed the principle clearly enough.

If you would be wealthy, said Father Abraham, you must think of saving as well as of getting, and the order in which he put the words was deliberate. Making money is only half of the task, since a purse with a hole in the bottom is empty however much is poured in. It is the second half, he said, that most of us neglect, and it is the half that decides how things end.

The Indies have not made Spain rich, said Father Abraham, because her outgoings have been greater than her incomings, and he used the great nation as a grand example of a small truth. The Spanish government received enormous quantities of gold and silver from its lands in the Americas, but it spent even more, and it went bankrupt more than once. A river of money will run dry if it flows out as fast as it flows in.

Away with your expensive follies, said Father Abraham, and you will not have so much cause to complain of hard times, of heavy taxes or of the cost of a growing family. The crowd had arrived believing that its troubles came from outside, and he was asking it to look at its own front door. Many of our burdens, he said, are bought in the shops and then carried home by our own hands.

Wine, gambling and deceit, said Father Abraham, make the wealth small and the want great, and he named them as the old almanack had done. These habits drain money out of the purse and trust out of a man's reputation, and when both are gone it is very hard to start again. He did not preach for long about them, for the audience knew the truth already.

What maintains one vice, said Father Abraham, would bring up two children, and the sentence had the weight of a hammer in it. He meant that a costly bad habit can eat up in a year the money that would have fed, clothed and schooled a pair of young people. The listeners fell silent, and several of the women looked pointedly at their husbands.

You may think, perhaps, said Father Abraham, that a little tea or a little punch now and then, a meal that is a little more costly, clothes a little finer and a little entertainment can be no great matter. The old man knew exactly how reasonable such thoughts sound, and for that very reason he did not agree with them. Remember, he told them, that small things have a stubborn way of adding up to something very large.

Many a little makes a mickle, said Father Abraham, using an old word for a large amount that his listeners knew from their grandmothers. A penny spent here and a penny spent there seem to be nothing at all, but pennies are good at multiplying when they travel in groups. By the end of the year, he warned, the little leaks have usually become a stream.

Beware of little expenses, said Father Abraham, for a small leak will sink a great ship, as Poor Richard says. Any sailor will tell you that the greatest dangers are often the ones that nobody has bothered to notice, since the sea needs only a crack and a little patience. A household's savings, he warned, are lost in exactly that quiet way, one small hole at a time.

Who dainties love shall beggars prove, said Father Abraham, and the word dainties meant delicate and costly foods of the kind that wealthy people eat. A person who has become used to such treats finds it hard to go back to bread and cheese, and he may be tempted to spend his last coin to avoid doing so. Such a taste, in short, is an expensive habit to keep, and it has emptied many a fine pocket.

Fools make feasts, said Father Abraham, and wise men eat them, and that put the whole matter very neatly in a single clause. The host who lays out a lavish dinner to impress his neighbours is out of pocket and weary, but the guest who sits at the table has lost nothing at all. There was laughter, because every person in the crowd could imagine being either one.

Here at this very sale, said Father Abraham, you are all got together to buy fineries and knick-knacks, which you call goods, but which, if you do not take care, will prove to be evils to some of you. He swept his hand toward the tables and the crowd turned to look at what they had come to buy. A few of them looked a little guilty, since the old man had put his finger on their hopes.

You expect that these goods will be sold cheap, said Father Abraham, and perhaps they will indeed be sold for less than they cost the merchant. But if you have no need of them, he explained, they must be dear to you at any price, since an unneeded thing is a loss however small the number written on it. The arithmetic of a bargain, he said, begins with the question of whether you wanted it.

Buy what thou hast no need of, said Father Abraham, quoting the old almanack in the old style, and ere long thou shalt sell thy necessaries. In plain words, the man who fills his house with extras may soon find that he has sold the bed that he sleeps on to pay for them. It is a bitter sort of joke, and a number of faces in the crowd twitched when they heard it.

At a great pennyworth, said Father Abraham, pause a while, and by a pennyworth he meant a bargain that looks too good to refuse. The cheapness, he explained, may only be apparent and not real, or else the bargain, by straining a man's resources in his business, may do him more harm than good. A man who is dazzled by a low price often forgets to ask what will be left in his pocket.

In another place, said Father Abraham, Poor Richard says that many have been ruined by buying good pennyworths. The danger, he explained, is not in the price itself but in the way that a bargain tempts us to spend what we had not planned to spend. The shopper who comes home with a heap of cheap things has still lost the money that paid for them.

It is foolish, said Father Abraham, to lay out money in a purchase of repentance, which is to say that a man buys the goods and then buys regret to go with them. This folly is practised every day at sales just like this one, he said, for want of minding the almanack. The people around him smiled nervously, because they could all hear how thoughtfully he had used Poor Richard's name.

Many a one, said Father Abraham, has gone about with a hungry belly for the sake of finery on his back, and has half-starved his family to pay for it. There are men in every town who dress like gentlemen and dine on crusts, and women who go to church in silk and go home to a cold hearth. He did not name anyone in the crowd, but then he did not need to, because the faces told the whole story.

Silks and satins, scarlet and velvet, said Father Abraham, put out the kitchen fire, as Poor Richard says, and the line has been quoted ever since. The picture is a clear one, in which money spent on rich cloth is money that is no longer buying wood for the hearth or meat for the pot. A fine dress looks magnificent in the street, but it cannot warm a cold house.

These things are not the necessaries of life, said Father Abraham, and they can scarcely be called the conveniences, and yet only because they look pretty, how many people want to have them! The crowd looked at the tables of fine goods that were laid out for the sale, and several of them wondered what they had meant to buy. It is hard to resist a handsome thing when it is displayed in a good light.

In this way, said Father Abraham, the artificial wants of mankind become more numerous than the natural ones. Our real needs are few and quickly counted, being food, warmth, clothing and shelter, but the things we imagine that we want are as numberless as the stars. A man who tries to satisfy them all will never be able to stop working long enough to enjoy anything.

As Poor Richard says, said Father Abraham, for one poor person there are a hundred indigent, and by indigent he meant people who are in need of things. He seemed to be saying that the wants we invent for ourselves leave a great many people poor who need not be so, and that more people suffer from wanting too much than from having too little. It was a hard saying, and some in the crowd frowned at it, but it seemed to the old man to be perfectly true.

By these and other extravagances, said Father Abraham, the genteel are reduced to poverty and forced to borrow from those whom they formerly despised, but who, through industry and frugality, have maintained their standing. The gentleman who once looked down on his hard-working neighbour now stands at the neighbour's door with his hat in his hand. It is one of the oldest reversals in the world, and one of the most humbling.

A ploughman on his legs, said Father Abraham, is higher than a gentleman on his knees, and the farmers in the crowd stood a little straighter. A man who earns his own bread and owes nothing to anyone, he explained, stands taller than a man of high birth who has been brought to beg for a loan. Dignity, he suggested, is not a matter of clothing or of birth but of independence, and that is a possession which no tailor can sell.

Perhaps they have had a small estate left to them, said Father Abraham, and since they knew nothing about the labour of getting it, they have little idea how to keep it. They think that it is day and will never be night, and that a little to be spent out of so much is not worth minding. Every fortune, he said, meets its sunset sooner or later, and the darkness that follows is a cold and unforgiving one.

Always taking out of the meal tub, and never putting in, said Father Abraham, soon comes to the bottom. A fortune that is only spent and never added to will run out far sooner than anyone has calculated, and the people who have been drawing from it will be startled by how hollow it sounds. A meal tub, like a purse, is a fine servant but a poor magician.

When the well's dry, said Father Abraham, they know the worth of water, and he told it as a plain fact about human nature. Human beings tend to prize a blessing only after it has been lost, and by that time there may be nothing left but regret. He added that the wretched lesson could have been avoided altogether had they heeded Poor Richard's advice.

If you would know the value of money, said Father Abraham, go and try to borrow some, and the old man spoke as if he had once tried it himself. A borrower learns very quickly how hard money is to come by, how closely it is guarded and how much it can cost in humble words and favours. The lesson is a cheaper one when it is learned before the loan, not after.

He that goes a-borrowing goes a-sorrowing, said Father Abraham, and he added with a dry smile that so does the man who lends to such people, when he goes to get it back. A loan, in other words, is a small cloud that hangs over both parties, and it often spoils a friendship before it is paid. Few debts are truly forgotten, he said, and fewer still are forgiven cheerfully by those who are still waiting.

Poor Dick, as the old man called the almanack's author, farther advises that fond pride of dress is sure a very curse, and that ere fancy you consult, you should consult your purse. The rhyme is meant to be said at the moment when one stands in a shop and wants something dazzling. A short look at the purse, he said, has saved many a foolish purchase.

Pride is as loud a beggar as want, said Father Abraham, and a great deal more saucy, which is to say that it is rude as well as expensive. A man who is poor from real need may ask with humility, but a man who is poor from pride demands what he wants as if it were a right and then complains of the price. Want, at least, is honest in its asking, and it is seldom ashamed to be seen for what it is.

When you have bought one fine thing, said Father Abraham, you must buy ten more, that your appearance may be all of a piece. A new hat makes the old coat look shabby, and a new coat makes the old shoes look worse, until the poor man has refitted himself from head to foot at a cost he can never afford. The first purchase, the old man warned, is only the beginning of a very long and very expensive road.

It is easier, said Poor Dick, to suppress the first desire than to satisfy all those that follow it, and Father Abraham repeated the line slowly so that everyone could take it in. Once a wish has been granted, it brings a flock of younger wishes after it, and each one is a little more expensive than the last. The cheapest way to be satisfied, he suggested, is to begin by saying no, and to go on saying it.

It is as truly folly, said Father Abraham, for the poor to ape the rich as for the frog to swell in order to equal the ox, and he made a small gesture of a puffed-up cheek. In the old fable the frog blows itself up in imitation of a large animal and does itself nothing but harm. The point is that the effort to seem grand will hurt those who cannot afford it.

Vessels large may venture more, said Father Abraham, but little boats should keep near shore, and the sailors among his listeners nodded at the good sense of it. A rich man can take a risk that would sink a poor man, and a poor man who sails like a rich one will soon find himself in a storm. The wise course, he said, is to live within the size of one's own boat and to be content with the shallow water.

It is a folly that is soon punished, said Father Abraham, for pride that dines on vanity sups on contempt, as Poor Richard says. A person who struts about at midday, hoping to impress his neighbours, may find by evening that they are smiling behind their hands and thinking of him with scorn. Vanity is a thin sort of dinner, and the bill for it is paid in respect.

And in another place, said Father Abraham, Poor Richard says that pride breakfasted with Plenty, dined with Poverty and supped with Infamy, and the old man gave each of the three meals a different weight of voice. The proud man's day begins in abundance, passes through want and ends in shame, so that the three courses of a short life are served in the wrong order. The crowd, which had been following every word with great attention since he began to speak, murmured in agreement.

And after all, asked Father Abraham, what is the use of this pride of appearance, for which so much is risked and so much is suffered? He waited, and the crowd, which had been so quick to nod, found that it did not have a ready answer. It is a remarkable thing, he said, how much we pay for the opinion of people who are not paying attention.

Pride of appearance cannot promote health, said Father Abraham, nor can it ease pain, and he looked about at the weathered faces around him. A man in a silk coat suffers from the same fever as a man in a woollen one, and the grave is no respecter of tailoring. Whatever the clothes may do for the eye, they do nothing for the body that wears them.

It makes no increase of merit in the person, said Father Abraham, it creates envy, and it hastens misfortune, and he counted the three evils on his fingers. A showy man gains no real virtue from his show, and the neighbours who look at him are more often jealous than admiring. The goods that were bought to impress, he said, tend to attract the very wrong sort of attention.

But what madness it must be, said Father Abraham, to run in debt for these superfluities, and the word came out as bluntly as a slammed door. It is one thing to spend from your own purse, he said, however foolishly, but it is quite another to spend what you do not have and will have to find later. Debt, in short, takes the folly of the purchase and adds to it the further folly of the promise.

We are offered, said Father Abraham, by the terms of this vendue, six months' credit, and that offer has perhaps brought some of us here, because we cannot spare the ready money and hope to be fine without it. A promise of later payment feels like a gift, but it is only a loan with a smile on its face. Never in the history of trade, he said dryly, has a merchant offered a loan out of pure kindness.

Ah, but think what you do when you run in debt, said Father Abraham, for you give another person power over your liberty. The lender does not need to use that power at once, and he may even smile and say that there is no hurry, but the power is his from the moment that the promise is made. A free man has been turned into a man who must always watch the calendar.

If you cannot pay at the time that was promised, said Father Abraham, you will be ashamed to see your creditor, and you will be in fear when you speak to him. You will begin to cross the road to avoid his house and to look for another way around the market square. A man who must hide from his neighbour has already lost more than the sum that he owes.

You will make poor, pitiful, sneaking excuses, said Father Abraham, and by degrees you will come to lose your veracity and sink into base, downright lying. The first untruth is a small and almost harmless one, such as the claim that the money is coming next week, but each lie must be defended by another. At the far end of that chain, the man's good name is quite gone, and with it the trust of the whole town.

The second vice is lying, said Father Abraham, and the first is running in debt, as Poor Richard truly says. He did not claim that every debtor was a liar, but that debt leads many a decent person into the next vice, and the second step is easier because the first has been taken. Few of us fall from the top of a staircase in a single stride.

Again to the same purpose, said Father Abraham, lying rides upon debt's back, whereas a free person ought not to be ashamed or afraid to see or speak to anyone living. Father Abraham thought of the free citizen as something precious, and he did not want to see his hearers throw that dignity away for the sake of a handsome waistcoat. To walk down the street without fear, he said, is a kind of wealth.

But poverty often deprives a man of all spirit and virtue, said Father Abraham, and he quoted Poor Richard's remark that it is hard for an empty bag to stand upright. A sack with nothing in it falls flat on the floor, and a man with nothing in his pocket may find that his courage slumps in the same way. The point was not to despise the poor but to avoid joining them through folly.

What would you think, said Father Abraham, of a prince or of a government that should issue an order forbidding you to dress like a gentleman or gentlewoman, on pain of imprisonment or servitude? Would you not say that you are free, that you have a right to dress as you please, and that such an order would be a breach of your privileges? The listeners growled that of course they would, and several of them shouted that they would never put up with it.

And yet, said Father Abraham, you are about to put yourself under exactly that tyranny when you run in debt for such dress, and the crowd, which had been growling, went quiet. A man who would resist an unjust law with all his strength will sign a piece of paper at the draper's counter, never noticing that it binds him just as tightly. The only difference, he said, is that nobody forces you to sign, and so the chain is fastened by your own hand.

In those days the law was hard on debtors, said Father Abraham, and a creditor had authority to deprive you of your liberty, at his pleasure, by shutting you up in gaol, perhaps for life. He might even sell you to work as a servant until the sum had been paid, if you were not able to find the money. These were not threats made for effect, but the actual law of the land.

When you have got your bargain, said Father Abraham, you may perhaps think very little of payment, and you may even forget the day. But creditors, as Poor Richard tells us, have better memories than debtors, and a man who lends money has a very fine head for dates. In this matter, he warned, only one side of the table ever forgets, and it is never the side that holds the ledger.

In another place, said Father Abraham, Poor Richard says that creditors are a superstitious sect, great observers of set days and times. Superstitious people, he meant, attach a special importance to particular dates and will not let one go by without notice, and a lender behaves in exactly that manner about the day when his money was promised. Nobody in the whole history of commerce has ever heard of a forgetful creditor, he added, and the crowd laughed at the thought.

The day comes round, said Father Abraham, before you are aware of it, and the demand is made before you are prepared to satisfy it. A debt that seemed to belong to the far end of the year turns up one morning on the doorstep, with its hat in its hand and a patient but unyielding look. There is no such thing, he said, as a debt that has gone away by itself.

Or if you bear your debt in mind, said Father Abraham, the term that at first seemed so long will, as it grows shorter, appear extremely short indeed. Time itself, he said, will seem to have added wings to his heels as well as to his shoulders, and the last month of a loan passes in about a week. Anyone who has waited for a bill to fall due will know exactly what he meant.

Those have a short Lent, saith Poor Richard, who owe money to be paid at Easter, and Father Abraham said the line with a smile. Lent is the forty days of fasting and prayer that come before the spring festival of Easter, and it can seem a long time to those who are giving up their dinners. To a debtor with a payment due on Easter morning, however, those forty days pass in a flash.

Since the borrower is a slave to the lender, said Father Abraham, and the debtor to the creditor, he urged his listeners to disdain the chain, to preserve their freedom and to maintain their independence. Be industrious and free, he said, and be frugal and free, and he said it so that the two words rang together like two notes in a chord. It was the central idea of the whole speech, and the crowd was very still.

At present, said Father Abraham, some of you may think yourselves in thriving circumstances, well able to bear a little extravagance without any injury to your affairs. He looked slowly round the circle, as though he could see through each coat to the purse beneath it. The comfortable, he suggested, are exactly the people who most need to hear what comes next.

But for age and for want, said Father Abraham, save while you may, for no morning sun lasts a whole day. Every farmer knows that a fair sunrise says little about the weather at noon, and every almanack reader knew that Poor Richard had made a living out of guessing it. Good fortune, he warned, is only a forecast, and a forecast has never yet been a promise.

Gain may be temporary and uncertain, said Father Abraham, but as long as you live, expense is constant and certain. A harvest can fail, a customer can disappear and a ship can go down with its cargo, yet the baker still wants his money on the morning that the bread is bought. Income is a visitor, he said, but spending is a member of the household.

It is easier to build two chimneys, said Father Abraham, than to keep one of them in fuel. A man may find the money to put up a handsome house in a single season, but the wood, the candles and the servants will go on eating his income for the rest of his days. The cost of starting, he said, is a small thing next to the cost of continuing.

So rather go to bed without your supper, said Father Abraham, than rise in debt in the morning. An empty stomach is a trouble that the night will mend, but a debt keeps its place on the table all through the dark and wakes up before you do. It was an old rule of the thrifty, and he gave it the force of a law.

Keep a plain account of what you earn and what you spend, said Father Abraham, and look at it as often as you look at the sky. A small leak can be mended only by a man who knows where it is, and a purse that is never counted is a purse that is always leaking. It is a humble habit, but it has saved a great many households from ruin.

Even a few pennies put aside every week, said Father Abraham, will in time grow into a useful sum, because many a little makes a mickle. Nobody is asked to save a fortune in a single day, and nobody should be ashamed of a small beginning, provided that it is made today and not next year. The first coin in the jar, he said, is the hardest, and the rest follow it more easily.

Get what you can, said Father Abraham, and what you get hold, for that, in the words of Poor Richard, is the stone that will turn all your lead into gold. Having earned a shilling by honest work, a man should keep it from the grasp of idle spending. The saying was a little riddle, and the crowd waited to hear him explain it.

For many centuries men called alchemists hunted for a philosopher's stone, a magical substance that was supposed to turn common lead into precious gold. They spent whole lives and fortunes over their furnaces, and not one of them ever succeeded in making a single coin. Father Abraham knew that his listeners had heard the old tales, and he used them to make his point.

The real philosopher's stone, said Father Abraham, is nothing but industry and frugality joined together, and the man who owns it need not go looking for the other one. When you have got it, he told them, you will no longer complain of bad times or of the difficulty of paying taxes. The crowd had come to grumble about the government, and they found that the old man had given the question back to them.

This doctrine, my friends, said Father Abraham, is reason and wisdom, and I have given it to you as plainly as I can. Then his voice dropped, and the people at the back of the crowd pressed forward, for they could tell that he was about to add something different. A good teacher, he knew, always saves the gentlest lesson for the very last, when his listeners are ready for it.

But after all, said Father Abraham, do not depend too much upon your own industry, frugality and prudence, excellent things though they are. A man who believes that his own effort alone has made him safe is a man who has forgotten how many things lie outside his control. Pride in one's work, he implied, can turn into a blindness of its own.

They may all be blasted, said Father Abraham, without the blessing of Heaven, and every person in the crowd could think of an example. A hailstorm can flatten a field of ripe corn within an hour, a fire can reduce a shop to ashes in a night, and an illness can take away a strong man's ability to earn. Foresight, he said, can reduce such dangers a great deal, but it can never remove them altogether, and it is foolish to pretend otherwise.

Therefore, said Father Abraham, ask for that blessing humbly, as a person asks for a gift and not as a person claims a debt. In the language of his day, Heaven meant God, and the old man spoke as a believer would, without any desire to argue with the unbelieving. The point of the advice, however, is one that people of every belief can understand.

The rich merchants and the poor farmers stood shoulder to shoulder in the crowd, and for a moment the difference in their coats seemed to matter very little. The old man had said nothing about rank or birth, because his warning applied to anybody who owned a field, a shop or a purse. It is easier to listen to advice, as every teacher knows, when it is plainly meant for everyone.

And be not uncharitable, said Father Abraham, to those who at present seem to want that blessing, but comfort them and help them as well as you are able. A speech about thrift might have ended with a sneer at the poor, and the old man chose to end it with kindness instead. The listeners who had been nodding at his sharpest sayings now looked a little ashamed.

Not everyone who is poor has become so through folly, and the old man was careful to say it before he sat down. Sickness, a failed harvest, a flood or a war can ruin the most careful family in a village, and such people deserve comfort and help rather than a lecture. The speech, he made clear, was against waste and idleness and had never been against misfortune, which can strike anyone.

Remember that Job suffered, said Father Abraham, and was afterwards prosperous, and think of that when you meet a neighbour in trouble. Job is the man in the Bible who lost his flocks, his house and his health, and whose long patience was rewarded when his fortunes were restored at the end. The reminder was a gentle one, and it said that a hard season is not the same as a hard life.

Franklin tried to live by this lesson, and in 1736 he helped to found a volunteer fire company in Philadelphia, the Union Fire Company. Its members agreed to hurry to a neighbour's burning house with buckets and bags, and to help to save the goods of a member in distress. It was a sensible kind of insurance, built out of friendship and not of money.

In 1751 he joined his friend Dr Thomas Bond in the founding of a hospital in Philadelphia, the Pennsylvania Hospital, which was meant to care for the sick. Poor people who could not pay were to be treated there as well, and the money came partly from gifts by citizens. For Franklin, a man's own industry and the help of his neighbours were never two separate ideas.

And now to conclude, said Father Abraham, experience keeps a dear school, but fools will learn in no other, and scarce in that. He said it with a smile, because every person in the crowd had paid some of its fees at one time or another. All around him there was a murmur of rueful nods, and a few sheepish laughs.

A dear school, in the old sense of the word, is a costly one, and the fees of this particular school are paid in lost money, lost time and lost goodwill. Nobody enters it by choice, and nobody leaves it without a few lessons that he could have learned more cheaply from a book. The old man said that he wished, if he could, to spare his listeners the bill, or at least to make it smaller.

The cheapest lessons are the ones that we take from other people's mistakes, since the neighbour who falls into the ditch has paid the fee on our behalf. A sensible traveller watches where the cart goes off the road and steers a little wider on his own journey. It costs nothing except a little attention, which is exactly what fools refuse to spend.

It is true, said Father Abraham, that we may give advice, but we cannot give conduct. By conduct he meant the daily habit of acting well, which no friend and no almanack can lend to another person, however kindly it is offered. The rule can be handed across the table, but the living of it must be done by the one who takes it.

Knowing what to do is a very different matter from doing it, as anybody who has made a resolution on the first of January will agree. The best rule in the world is useless to a person who never puts it into practice, and a wise saying does no work until somebody carries it out. Abraham was telling his listeners that the hard part of his speech would begin when they walked away.

However, remember this, said Father Abraham, that they who will not be counselled cannot be helped. A friend may point out the right road a hundred times, but he cannot make a stubborn traveller take a single step along it. The old man had done everything that an adviser can do, and now the next move belonged to his hearers.

And further, said Father Abraham, if you will not hear Reason, she will surely rap your knuckles, and a ripple of laughter ran through the crowd. Many of them could still remember a schoolmistress with a ruler in her hand, and the picture of Reason as that same fierce lady was one they understood very well. The hearer who ignores good sense, he said, will be taught by something much less gentle.

Father Abraham looked slowly around the crowd with a kind smile, and the sharpness that had been in his voice a minute earlier was gone. He had spoken bluntly at times, but it was plain to every listener that he spoke from care for them and not from scorn. People forgive a great deal of plain speaking from someone who obviously wants their good.

He had said everything that he wanted to say, and he thanked the people for their patient attention in a few quiet words. Then he stepped back, put on his hat and fell silent, like a man who has set down a heavy load at a friend's door, and he asked for nothing in return. Several people looked as though they wished to thank him, but they did not quite know how to begin.

For a moment the whole crowd was quiet, and it seemed that the old man had touched something that each of them had always half known. Everyone had been given a great deal to think about, from the tax collector's bill to the cost of a silk coat, and nobody wished to speak first. The silence was the best praise that the speech was ever going to receive.

So the old gentleman ended his speech, and Richard Saunders, who had listened to every word from the back of his horse, watched the crowd begin to stir. The silence broke into a hum of talk as the people turned to one another, and the little groups formed and re-formed around the square. Richard, like a good author, was curious to learn what his old friend had made of them.

The people had heard the speech, and they approved the doctrine with every sign of sincerity, shaking their heads over the folly of wasteful neighbours. Many of them said to one another that every word had been exactly right, and some even promised to tell their children. It is easy to agree with a sermon, as anybody knows who has ever sat in a church pew.

And yet they immediately practised the contrary, just as if the speech had been a common sermon heard on a Sunday and forgotten by dinner. The same good neighbours who had nodded at every saying began to push towards the tables where the goods were waiting. Whatever the old man had hoped for, he must have known better than to expect it.

For the vendue opened at that very moment, and the people began to buy with the greatest extravagance, as if the speech had never been given. Hands went up all over the square, and the bidding rose and rose as one neighbour tried to outdo another. The auctioneer, who had stood and heard the speech with a patient face, must have been the happiest man in the town.

A gilded looking glass, a length of bright silk and a set of fine cups were all knocked down in the first hour, each one to a buyer who had just agreed that such things were folly. Many of them could hardly afford the prices that they had cried out so eagerly, and some had bought on six months' credit. The lender, as Poor Richard had warned them only a few minutes earlier, would certainly remember the day.

Richard Saunders sat quietly on his horse and thought about everything he had just heard. It dawned on him that the good old man had studied his almanacks thoroughly, and that every point in the speech came from them. He was surprised, and a little moved, to learn that anybody had read them with such steady attention.

Richard recognised sayings that he had scattered through the pages of his almanack over twenty-five years, one here and one there, like seeds dropped on a path. Now they had been gathered into a single harvest and spoken aloud by a stranger in a clear and steady voice. A writer who hears his scattered work made whole in this way has every right to feel astonished.

Richard was delighted to hear his sayings so well repeated, and he admits as much without the least embarrassment. As he had written in his preface, nothing pleases an author more than to find his works respectfully quoted by others, and here he had been quoted by a crowd. His pride, though, was the sort that can be turned to good use, if its owner has the sense to try.

Yet Richard did not let his pride carry him away, for he had a wiser thought as he sat there among the shouting bidders. He resolved to be the better for the echo of his own sayings, and to put into practice what the old man had said in his name. An author, he saw, is the last person who should ignore his own book.

Richard had meant at first to buy cloth for a new coat that very day, and the shilling was already in his hand. Instead he put it back in his pocket, turned his horse for home and decided to wear his old coat a little longer. If his readers will do the same, he says, their profit will be as great as his.

Richard ended his preface as he had ended so many others, by signing himself the humble servant of his reader, Richard Saunders. Behind that cheerful old name sat Benjamin Franklin, the real author of the whole performance, quietly enjoying his own joke. Few readers of the almanack suspected that the little tale had so busy a printer behind it.

The speech first appeared in the almanack for 1758, and it was so popular that other printers soon began to print it by itself, as a small pamphlet and on large single sheets for pinning to a wall. Each time it travelled a little further, from one town and one colony to the next. Franklin never needed to advertise it very much, because its own readers did that work for him, and they did it for nothing.

In 1757, a year before the speech appeared in print, Franklin sailed across the Atlantic to London, where he was to speak for the colony of Pennsylvania. He spent much of the following eighteen years living in England, and he took his reputation as a clever writer with him. The little almanack man from Philadelphia was becoming a figure on the wider stage.

By then his experiments with electricity had made him famous across Europe, and his invention of the lightning rod had begun to protect church towers and houses from the stroke of the storm. Scientists who had never heard of Poor Richard knew Franklin's name and admired his clear way of explaining. The man who could reduce a thunderbolt to plain words had little trouble with a sale.

In 1776 Franklin, by then an old man, was one of the men who signed the Declaration of Independence, which announced that the American colonies were free of British rule. Before the year was out he had crossed the ocean once more, this time to France, to ask that country for friendship and help in the war. He was seventy years old, and the French were charmed by the plain old philosopher.

In the 1770s the sayings of Poor Richard were also printed in French, in a little book known as La Science du Bonhomme Richard, which means roughly The Science of Good Man Richard. From French the speech passed into many other languages, and it was soon being read in countries that Franklin had never visited. Readers everywhere seemed to enjoy being scolded by a wise old man for their own good.

In 1779 the American naval officer John Paul Jones named his warship Bonhomme Richard, in honour of Franklin and of the French name by which Poor Richard was now known. It was an odd kind of tribute, since the ship was a fighting vessel and its namesake was a man who preached thrift and peace. Yet it shows how far the old almanack character had travelled from a Philadelphia print shop.

In 1783 Franklin was one of the Americans who agreed the Treaty of Paris, which ended the war with Britain and recognised the new country. Two years later, in 1785, he sailed home to Philadelphia, where the citizens welcomed back a man who had spent so many years abroad. He was about seventy-nine years old by then, and he was still full of plans for his city and his country.

Franklin died in Philadelphia on 17 April 1790, at the age of eighty-four, after a long life as a printer, writer, scientist and statesman. He left behind his Autobiography, the lively story of his own life, which he had worked on for years and never quite finished. Among the thousands of words that he wrote, however, few have had a longer career than the sayings of a made-up almanack maker.

Few pieces of advice have been printed so often or in so many languages as this speech, which has been read in many countries for more than two hundred years. Its message is plain: work steadily, spend with care, stay out of debt and save a little for the days when work is hard. Whether or not a reader ever grows rich, he will be wise to remember Poor Richard's old lesson that small savings are the first step toward freedom.
